challenges.prompt: A booking page lists slots in time order as `{ time, booked }`. Write `firstFree(slots)`, returning the `time` of the first slot that is not booked, using `find`. `find` gives `undefined` when nothing matches; return `null` then, so the page can say it is fully booked.
challenges.firstHint: `find` returns the first element its callback accepts, the whole element, or `undefined` when none is accepted. Read `.time` only once you know a slot was found.

challenges.title: Flatten every level
challenges.prompt: Write `flattenAll(list)`, returning a new array with every level of nesting removed, however deep it goes. `flat()` removes one level; pass it `Infinity` to remove them all. `flattenAll([1, [2, [3, [4]]]])` gives `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. Empty inner arrays disappear, and `list` is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: `flat(depth)` removes `depth` levels of nesting and returns a new array. `Infinity` is a number, so `flat(Infinity)` keeps going until nothing is nested.

challenges.title: A 404 is still a response
challenges.prompt: `fetch` rejects only when the request cannot be made at all. A 404 or a 500 still resolves to a response, with `ok` set to `false`. Write an `async` function `getJson(request, url)`, where `request` works like `fetch`: call it with the URL and await the response. When `response.ok` is `false`, throw an `Error` whose message is `"Request failed: "` followed by `response.status`. Otherwise return the body from `await response.json()`.
challenges.firstHint: A response says whether it succeeded in `response.ok`, which is `true` for statuses 200 to 299. `fetch` does not look at the status for you, so a missing page arrives as a normal response unless you check.

challenges.title: Spot the differences
challenges.prompt: Two grids have the same number of rows, and each row is the same length in both. Write `differences(a, b)`, returning the `[row, column]` position of every cell where the grids differ, compared with `!==`, row by row and left to right. Use one loop over the rows and a second loop inside it over that row’s columns. `differences([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[1, 0], [3, 5]])` gives `[[0, 1], [1, 1]]`. Identical grids give `[]`.
challenges.firstHint: The outer loop picks a row and the inner loop walks across it. The inner loop’s limit is the length of the current row, `a[row].length`, which need not equal the number of rows.

challenges.title: Add a header and a footer
challenges.prompt: A table is an array of rows. Write `framed(rows, header, footer)`, returning a new array with `header` first, then every row, then `footer`, using `concat`. `framed(["a", "b"], "Name", "End")` gives `["Name", "a", "b", "End"]`. A row, the header or the footer can itself be an array of cells, and each one stays a single item. `rows` is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: `concat` adds the items of any array you pass it, one level deep, and adds anything else as it is. Wrap the footer in brackets, `[footer]`, so a footer that is itself an array still arrives as one item.

challenges.title: Where does it go?
challenges.prompt: Write `insertAt(sorted, value)` for a list of numbers in ascending order, returning the index where `value` should go to keep the list sorted: the index of the first number that is greater than or equal to `value`. Use `findIndex`. When every number is smaller, `findIndex` gives -1, but the value belongs at the end, so return `sorted.length`. `insertAt([10, 20, 30], 25)` gives 2.
challenges.firstHint: `findIndex` returns the position of the first element its callback accepts, or -1. Here -1 means "after everything", which is the index `sorted.length`.

challenges.title: The last few
challenges.prompt: Write `lastFew(items, n)`, returning a new array of the last `n` items, using `slice` with a negative start. `lastFew(["a", "b", "c", "d"], 2)` gives `["c", "d"]`. Asking for more items than there are gives them all. Watch one edge: an `n` of 0 must give `[]`, but `slice(-0)` is the same as `slice(0)` and copies the whole array.
challenges.firstHint: A negative start counts back from the end: `slice(-2)` copies the last two items. `-0` is the same number as `0`, so `slice(-0)` copies everything.

challenges.title: Letters in the same order
challenges.prompt: Write `inOrder(short, long)`, returning `true` when every character of `short` appears in `long` in the same order, though not necessarily side by side. `inOrder("ace", "abcde")` gives `true`, and `inOrder("aec", "abcde")` gives `false`. Keep one index in each string: move the `long` index on every step, and move the `short` index only when the two characters match. Each character of `long` can be used once. An empty `short` is always in order.
challenges.firstHint: The two indexes move at different speeds. `j` visits every character of `long`; `i` only moves when it finds the character it is waiting for. If `i` reaches `short.length`, every character was found in order.

challenges.title: Mirror images
challenges.prompt: Write `isMirror(a, b)`, returning `true` when `b` holds the items of `a` in reverse order. Walk with two indexes: one moves forwards through `a` from the start, the other backwards through `b` from the end, and stop at the first pair that differs. Lists of different lengths are never mirrors. `isMirror([1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1])` gives `true`. Neither list is changed.
challenges.firstHint: Start `i` at 0 and `j` at `b.length - 1`, then move them in opposite directions. Check the lengths first: a shorter `b` can match every pair you compare and still not be a mirror.

challenges.title: What comes next
challenges.prompt: A checkout runs through fixed steps, such as `["cart", "address", "payment", "done"]`. Write `nextStep(steps, current)`, returning the step after `current`, using `indexOf` to find where `current` is. The last step has no next step, and neither does a name that is not in the list: return `null` for both.
challenges.firstHint: `indexOf` gives -1 when the value is missing, and `-1 + 1` is 0, so an unknown step would return the first step with no error. Check for -1 before you use the index.

challenges.title: Even places and odd places
challenges.prompt: Write `placeTotals(numbers)`, returning `{ even, odd }`: the sum of the numbers at even positions (0, 2, 4 and so on) and the sum of those at odd positions (1, 3, 5 and so on). Use `forEach`, whose callback receives each number’s index as its second argument. `placeTotals([5, 1, 4, 2])` gives `{ even: 9, odd: 3 }`. The position decides, not whether the number is even. An empty array gives `{ even: 0, odd: 0 }`.
challenges.firstHint: `forEach` calls your function with the value, then its index, then the whole array. `index % 2 === 0` is true at positions 0, 2, 4 and so on.

challenges.title: Send JSON with a POST
challenges.prompt: Write an `async` function `postJson(request, url, data)`, where `request` works like `fetch`. Call it with the URL and an options object with these three properties and no others: `method: "POST"`, `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }`, and `body`, which is `data` turned into JSON text with `JSON.stringify`. Await the response and return its `status`, whatever it is.
challenges.firstHint: A request body travels as text, so an object has to go through `JSON.stringify` first. The `Content-Type` header tells the server how to read that text.

challenges.title: Only the public fields
challenges.prompt: Write `toPublicJson(user)`, returning the user as JSON text that holds only `id`, `name` and `avatar`, in that order, so nothing private such as `email` leaves the server. `JSON.stringify` takes an array of property names as its second argument and writes only those, in the order listed. A listed field the user does not have is left out.
challenges.firstHint: The second argument of `JSON.stringify` is called the replacer. Given an array of strings, it works as an allow-list: every other property is left out of the text.

challenges.title: Recent searches
challenges.prompt: A search box shows the latest searches first and remembers at most `max` of them. Write `addSearch(recent, term, max)`, which puts `term` at the front of `recent` with `unshift`, then removes searches from the end with `pop` until no more than `max` are left. It changes `recent` in place and returns it. `addSearch(["css", "html"], "js", 2)` gives `["js", "css"]`.
challenges.firstHint: `unshift` adds to the front and moves every other item one place along. `pop` takes the last, oldest item off. A `while` loop keeps popping for as long as the list is too long.

challenges.title: Record every call
challenges.prompt: Write `recorded(fn, calls)`, returning a new function that does what `fn` does and also writes down each use. When the new function is called, it calls `fn` with the same arguments, pushes `{ args, result }` onto the `calls` array, and returns the result. Collect the arguments with a rest parameter, `(...args)`, so any number of them works. Nothing is written until the new function is called.
challenges.firstHint: A function that returns a function is a higher-order function. `(...args)` gathers every argument into an array, and `fn(...args)` spreads them back out as separate arguments.

challenges.title: A reminder for each event
challenges.prompt: Each event is `{ title, at }`, where `at` is a time in milliseconds on the same clock as `now`. Write `scheduleReminders(events, now, remind)`, which uses `forEach` to start one `setTimeout` per event, calling `remind(title)` when that event’s time comes, `at - now` milliseconds from now. An event at or before `now` has already started: skip it. Return how many reminders were scheduled.
challenges.firstHint: Each `setTimeout` runs on its own, so starting several at once is fine: they fire in order of their delays. The delay is the wait from now, `at - now`. Passing `at` itself would wait far too long.

challenges.title: Report what changed
challenges.prompt: Write `applyChanges(settings, changes, onChange)`. Go through the keys of `changes` with `for...in`. For each key whose new value differs from the one in `settings` (compare with `!==`), store the new value in `settings` and call `onChange(key, oldValue, newValue)`. A key whose value is already the same is left alone and not reported. Return how many keys changed.
challenges.firstHint: `for (const key in changes)` visits each key of `changes`. Read the old value before you overwrite it, or the callback will be told the new value twice.

challenges.title: Hide the spinner every time
challenges.prompt: Write an `async` function `withSpinner(show, hide, task)`. Call `show()`, then `await task()` and return what it resolves to. Call `hide()` in a `finally` block, so the spinner goes away once the task has finished, whether it succeeded or failed. When `task` rejects, `withSpinner` rejects with the same error, after hiding the spinner.
challenges.firstHint: A `finally` block runs after the `try` block, whether it returned or threw. It only waits for the task if the `try` block awaits it: `return task()` without `await` leaves the `try` block at once, and `finally` hides the spinner while the task is still running.

challenges.title: Split off the command
challenges.prompt: A chat bot reads a command as an array of words, such as `["add", "milk", "eggs"]`. Write `readCommand(words)`, returning `{ command, args }`: the first word as `command` and the words after it as `args`. Take the first word off a copy with `shift`, so the caller’s array is not changed. An empty array gives `{ command: null, args: [] }`.
challenges.firstHint: `shift` removes the first element and returns it, and every other element moves one place forward. It changes the array, which is why it runs on a copy here. On an empty array it returns `undefined`.

challenges.title: Count down, one tick at a time
challenges.prompt: Write `countdown(from, ms, onTick)`, which calls `onTick(from)` after `ms` milliseconds, then `onTick(from - 1)` `ms` milliseconds after that, and so on down to `onTick(1)`. Chain `setTimeout` calls rather than using `setInterval`: each tick schedules the next one, and the last tick schedules nothing. `countdown` itself returns straight away, before any tick. A `from` of 0 never calls `onTick`.
challenges.firstHint: `setTimeout(fn, ms)` runs `fn` once, later, and returns at once. A timer callback that starts another `setTimeout` makes a chain, and the chain stops when a callback starts nothing.

challenges.title: A number in binary
challenges.prompt: Write `toBinary(n)` for a whole number `n` of 0 or more, returning its binary digits as a string, with recursion rather than `toString(2)`. The last binary digit is `n % 2`, and the digits before it are the binary form of `Math.floor(n / 2)`. Stop when `n` is 0 or 1: it is its own single digit. `toBinary(6)` gives `"110"`.
challenges.firstHint: Every recursive function needs a base case that returns without calling itself. Here it is `n < 2`. Each other call halves `n`, so it always gets there.

challenges.title: Undo the last step
challenges.prompt: An editor keeps every change in a `history` array, oldest first. Write `undo(history)`, which removes the newest change from the end of the array with `pop` and returns it. The array gets shorter, so the next `undo` returns the change before. With nothing left to undo, return `null`: `pop` on an empty array gives `undefined`.
challenges.firstHint: `pop` removes the last element in place and returns it. On an empty array it returns `undefined`, so check the length first.

challenges.title: Even numbers
challenges.prompt: Write `evens(numbers)`, returning a new array of only the even values, in their original order. Zero counts as even, negatives are judged the same way, and an array with no even values gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: Even numbers have a remainder of 0 when divided by 2.

challenges.title: Event emitter
challenges.prompt: Write `createEmitter()`, returning an emitter with `on`, `off` and `emit`. `on` and `off` return the emitter so calls chain; `off(name, listener)` drops that one listener while `off(name)` drops every listener for that event; `emit(name, payload)` calls each listener with the payload and returns their results as an array.
challenges.firstHint: Keep an object of listener arrays, one per event name.

challenges.title: Find user
challenges.prompt: Write `findUser(users, name)`, returning the first user object whose `name` matches. Return `undefined` when nothing matches, or when the list is empty.
challenges.firstHint: You want the first element that matches, and the array method for that already returns undefined when nothing does — no extra handling needed.

challenges.title: First divisible
challenges.prompt: Write `firstDivisible(numbers, divisor)`, returning the first number in the array that divides by `divisor` with no remainder, or `null` when there is none. Walk the array with a `while` loop and use `break` the moment you find it. `firstDivisible([7, 9, 12, 20], 4)` gives 12, and zero is divisible by everything.
challenges.firstHint: Walk with an index while it is inside the array, and the moment the remainder is zero remember the value and break out — the loop condition alone would carry on to the end.

challenges.title: First letters
challenges.prompt: Write `firstLetters(words)`, returning an array of the first character of each word, in order and with its original case.
challenges.firstHint: One output per input again: each word becomes only its opening character, and a string can be indexed the way an array can.

challenges.title: Fizz values
challenges.prompt: Write `fizz(n)`, returning an array counting 1 to n where every multiple of 3 is replaced by the string `Fizz` — `fizz(5)` gives `[1, 2, “Fizz”, 4, 5]`. `fizz(0)` gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: Count from 1 up to n, and for each number decide whether it divides by three before you decide what to put in the array.

challenges.title: Flatten arrays
challenges.prompt: Write `flatten(arrays)`, returning one array holding the items of each inner array, in order. Flatten a single level only, and do it without `Array.prototype.flat`.
challenges.firstHint: Reduce by concatenating each inner array.

challenges.title: Frequency Map
challenges.prompt: Write `frequencies(values)`, returning a `Map` from each distinct value to how many times it appears, filled with `for…of` in first-seen order. `frequencies(["a", "b", "a"])` gives a Map with `"a"` → 2 and `"b"` → 1. Keys keep their type, so the number 1 and the string `"1"` are separate entries, and an empty array gives an empty Map.
challenges.firstHint: Read the current count with get, treat a missing one as zero, and write it back with set — a Map keeps the keys’ real types and their first-seen order.

challenges.title: Group by key
challenges.prompt: Write `groupBy(items, keyFn)`, returning an object that groups the items by whatever `keyFn` returns for each. That return becomes an object key — so numbers arrive as strings — and each value is the array of matching items, in order.
challenges.firstHint: Reduce into an object, pushing each item into its key’s array.

challenges.title: Handlers keep their index
challenges.prompt: Write `makeHandlers(count)`, returning an array of `count` functions built in a `for` loop whose counter is declared with `let`, so that the function at position i returns i when called — the way click handlers made in a loop each remember their own index. `makeHandlers(3).map(handler => handler())` gives `[0, 1, 2]`. A count of zero gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: Declare the loop variable with let: each pass of the loop then gets its own binding, so a function created inside remembers that pass’s index instead of the final value.

challenges.title: Has adult
challenges.prompt: Write `hasAdult(ages)`, returning true when at least one age is 18 or more. Exactly 18 counts; an empty array is false.
challenges.firstHint: You only need to know whether any single age qualifies, so the answer is a boolean and the search can stop the moment it finds one.

challenges.title: Highest with reduce
challenges.prompt: Write `highest(numbers)`, returning the largest value using `reduce`, with the accumulator holding the best value seen so far. `highest([3, 9, 2])` gives 9. It must work when every value is negative, and an empty array gives `null` — `reduce` with no initial value throws on one, so decide that case first.
challenges.firstHint: Let the accumulator be the best value so far; without an initial value reduce starts from the first element, which sidesteps the trap of starting from zero when everything is negative.

challenges.title: Immutable list edits
challenges.prompt: Write `withInserted(list, index, item)`, `withoutIndex(list, index)` and `withReplaced(list, index, item)`. Each returns a new array built from two `slice` copies spread into a fresh array literal, and never changes the array it was given. `withInserted([1, 3], 1, 2)` gives `[1, 2, 3]`, `withoutIndex([1, 2, 3], 0)` gives `[2, 3]`, and `withReplaced([1, 2, 3], 2, 9)` gives `[1, 2, 9]`.
challenges.firstHint: slice gives you the part before the index and the part from or after it, and spreading those two pieces into a new array literal — with or without the item between them — is the whole trick.

challenges.title: Insert at an index
challenges.prompt: Write `insertAt(list, index, item)`, inserting the item at that position in place with `splice` without removing anything, and returning the list. `insertAt([1, 3], 1, 2)` gives `[1, 2, 3]`. Index 0 puts the item first, and an index equal to the length appends it.
challenges.firstHint: splice can add as well as remove: a delete count of zero followed by the new item drops it in at the index without losing anything.

challenges.title: Join with for-of
challenges.prompt: Write `joinWords(words, separator)`, building one string with the separator between neighbouring words using a `for…of` loop rather than `join`. `joinWords(["a", "b", "c"], "-")` gives `"a-b-c"`. A single word gets no separator, and an empty array gives an empty string.
challenges.firstHint: Add a separator before every word except the first, and a flag or counter tells you which one is first.

challenges.title: Label numbers
challenges.prompt: Write `labelNumbers(numbers)`, returning a new array with the string `"positive"`, `"negative"` or `"zero"` for each number, decided by a ternary inside the `map` callback. `labelNumbers([3, -1, 0])` gives `["positive", "negative", "zero"]`. An empty array gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: A ternary is an expression, so it can be the whole body of the map callback, and a second ternary in its else branch decides the third label.

challenges.title: Largest number
challenges.prompt: Write `largest(numbers)`, returning the biggest value in the array. It must still work when every value is negative, and when the maximum appears more than once. Assume at least one number.
challenges.firstHint: Compare every value with the largest seen.

challenges.title: Last item safely
challenges.prompt: Write `lastItem(list, fallback)`, returning the last element of the list without changing it, or `fallback` when the list is empty. `lastItem([1, 2, 3], 0)` gives 3 and `lastItem([], "none")` gives `"none"`. A last element that happens to be falsy, such as 0, is still returned rather than the fallback.
challenges.firstHint: The last index is one less than the length, and only an empty list has no such index — deciding that first keeps the method that removes the item out of the picture.

challenges.title: Letter counts
challenges.prompt: Write `countLetters(text)`, returning an object mapping each character to how many times it appears — `countLetters(“aba”)` gives `{ a: 2, b: 1 }`. An empty string gives an empty object.
challenges.firstHint: Walk the characters building an object up as you go, treating a character you have not seen yet as though its count were already zero.

challenges.title: Locate an item
challenges.prompt: Write `locate(list, item)`, returning `{ present, index }`: whether the item is in the list, answered with `includes`, and the position of its first appearance, answered with `indexOf`, which is -1 when it is missing. `locate(["a", "b", "c"], "b")` gives `{ present: true, index: 1 }`. Both methods compare strictly, so the string `"1"` never matches the number 1.
challenges.firstHint: One method answers whether the item is there at all, the other tells you where it first appears and uses -1 for nowhere.

challenges.title: Longest word
challenges.prompt: Write `longest(words)`, returning the longest string in the array. When two are equally long, keep the one that comes first; an empty array returns an empty string.
challenges.firstHint: Walk the list keeping the best candidate found so far, and replace it only when the new word is strictly longer. That “strictly” is what leaves a tie on the earlier word.

challenges.title: LRU cache
challenges.prompt: Write `LRUCache(strArr)`, taking an array of letters that were accessed in order and returning what is left in a cache holding at most 5, joined with hyphens. Accessing a letter already in the cache moves it to the most recent end rather than adding it again; once the cache is full, the least recently used letter is dropped. `LRUCache(["A", "B", "A", "C", "A", "B"])` gives `"C-A-B"`.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the cache as an array with the most recently used letter last. A letter you have seen before is removed from where it was before being pushed back on.

challenges.title: Tally factory
challenges.prompt: Write `makeTally(start)`, returning a function that keeps a running total in the factory’s scope: each call takes any number of values, loops over them adding each to the total, and returns the new total. With `tally = makeTally(10)`, `tally(1, 2)` gives 13 and a later `tally(5)` gives 18. A call with no values returns the total as it is, and two tallies never share a total.
challenges.firstHint: The total lives in the factory’s scope, the returned function is the only thing that can reach it, and inside that function a loop over the rest parameter does the adding.

challenges.title: Map entries to pairs
challenges.prompt: Write `entriesAtLeast(map, min)`, returning an array of `[key, value]` pairs for every entry of the `Map` whose value is at least `min`, in insertion order, gathered with `for…of` over the Map and destructuring in the loop head. With `new Map([["a", 1], ["b", 5], ["c", 3]])` and a `min` of 3 it gives `[["b", 5], ["c", 3]]`. Nothing qualifying, or an empty Map, gives an empty array, and the Map is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: A Map is iterable and each turn of for-of gives an entry you can destructure into key and value; push a fresh two-item array for the ones that pass.

challenges.title: Matrix transpose
challenges.prompt: Write `transpose(matrix)`, returning a new matrix whose rows are the columns of the input, built with a `for` loop over the columns and an inner `for` loop over the rows; assume every row has the same length. `transpose([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])` gives `[[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]`. An empty matrix gives an empty array, and the input is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: Each column of the input becomes a row of the output, so let the outer loop walk the columns and the inner loop collect that column’s value from every row.

challenges.title: Memoize results
challenges.prompt: Write `memoize(fn)`, returning a wrapped function that caches by its first argument, so `fn` runs once per distinct argument. A falsy result is cached too, and each wrapper has its own cache.
challenges.firstHint: The wrapper needs somewhere to remember past answers between calls. Ask whether the key is present rather than whether the stored value is truthy, or a cached zero looks like a miss.

challenges.title: Upload in batches
challenges.prompt: Uploading 1,000 photos at once overloads the server, and uploading them one by one is slow. Write an `async` function `inBatches(items, size, worker)` that calls `worker(item)` for every item, `size` items at a time. `worker` returns a promise. Start a whole batch together, wait with `Promise.all` until every item in it has finished, and only then start the next batch. Cut the batches with `slice`. Resolve with all the results, in the same order as `items`. If a worker rejects, `inBatches` rejects with the same error and starts no further batch.
challenges.firstHint: `await` inside a `for` loop pauses the loop, so the next batch cannot start before the current one has finished.

challenges.title: Sort version numbers
challenges.prompt: Release tags such as `"1.10.0"` and `"1.9.2"` are whole numbers separated by dots. Sorted as text, `"1.10.0"` lands before `"1.9.2"`, because the character `1` comes before `9`. Write `sortVersions(versions)`, returning a new array from oldest to newest. Split each version on `"."`, turn the parts into numbers with `map`, and give `sort` a compare function that walks the parts from the left: the first part that differs decides. A missing part counts as 0, so `"2.1"` and `"2.1.0"` are equal, and equal versions keep the order they came in. Leave `versions` unchanged.
challenges.firstHint: A compare function returns a negative number when `a` comes first, a positive one when `b` does, and 0 when they are equal. `sort` keeps equal items in their original order, but only if you really return 0 for them.

challenges.title: Is this sudoku valid so far?
challenges.prompt: A sudoku board is 9 rows of 9 cells, each a digit from 1 to 9, or 0 for an empty cell. Write `isValidSudoku(board)`, returning `true` when no digit repeats within any row, any column or any of the nine 3 × 3 boxes. Empty cells never clash, and the board does not have to be complete or solvable. First check with `every` that the board has 9 rows of 9 cells, and return `false` if it does not. Then walk the board with two nested loops and remember what each row, column and box has seen in a `Set`, 27 sets in all. The box of cell `[r, c]` is number `Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3)`.
challenges.firstHint: `Array.from({ length: 9 }, () => new Set())` makes nine separate Sets. `new Array(9).fill(new Set())` would put the same Set in every place.

challenges.title: Write myMap and myFilter
challenges.prompt: Write `myMap(list, fn)` and `myFilter(list, fn)` with plain `for` loops instead of the built-in `map` and `filter`. `myMap` returns a new array of `fn(item, index)` results, and `myFilter` returns a new array of the items for which `fn(item, index)` is truthy; neither changes the list. `myMap([1, 2, 3], n => n * 2)` gives `[2, 4, 6]` and `myFilter([1, 2, 3, 4], n => n % 2 === 0)` gives `[2, 4]`.
challenges.firstHint: Both are a loop that calls the callback with the item and its index; map pushes whatever comes back, filter pushes the item only when what comes back is truthy.

challenges.title: Write myReduce
challenges.prompt: Write `myReduce(list, fn, initial)` with a plain `for` loop instead of the built-in `reduce`: call `fn(accumulator, item, index)` for each item, starting the accumulator at `initial`, and return the final accumulator. When `initial` is `undefined`, the first item becomes the starting accumulator and the loop begins at the second. `myReduce([1, 2, 3], (total, n) => total + n, 0)` gives 6, and an empty list with an initial value returns that value.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the accumulator in a variable, decide where the loop starts by whether an initial value was given, and let each pass replace the accumulator with the callback’s result.

challenges.title: Number the items
challenges.prompt: Write `numberItems(items)`, returning a new array where each item becomes a string of its one-based position, a dot, a space and the item, using `for…of` over `items.entries()` so the loop hands you the index and the value together. `numberItems(["milk", "eggs"])` gives `["1. milk", "2. eggs"]`, and an empty array gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: for-of alone gives you the value; ask the array for its entries and each turn hands you the index and the value together.

challenges.title: Number range
challenges.prompt: Write `range(start, end)`, returning every integer from start through end, both included. Start may equal end, and a negative start works the same way.
challenges.firstHint: Count up from start while you have not gone past end. The boundary is the whole exercise, because end is included in the result.

challenges.title: Object keys
challenges.prompt: Write `keys(object)`, returning an array of the object’s own key names in insertion order. An empty object gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: JavaScript hands you an object’s own key names as an array already — the question is which built-in returns the names rather than what is stored under them.

challenges.title: Object values
challenges.prompt: Write `values(object)`, returning an array of the object’s values in insertion order. `null` is a value like any other; an empty object gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: The same family of built-ins as the previous challenge, but this time you want what is stored rather than what it is stored under.

challenges.title: Odd sum
challenges.prompt: Write `oddSum(numbers)`, returning the total of just the odd values. Negative odds count; no odd values, or an empty array, totals 0.
challenges.firstHint: Two steps in sequence: decide which values qualify, then collapse those into a single total that starts from zero.

challenges.title: Total with defaults
challenges.prompt: Write `orderTotal(items)`, returning the total of `price` times `quantity` over every item, where a missing or `null` quantity means 1 — supplied with `??` inside a `for…of` loop. `orderTotal([{ price: 5 }, { price: 2, quantity: 3 }])` gives 11. A quantity of 0 is a real quantity and contributes nothing, and an empty order totals 0.
challenges.firstHint: The nullish operator supplies a default only for null and undefined, which is exactly why a quantity of zero survives it where the or operator would replace it.

challenges.title: Pair with a sum
challenges.prompt: Write `pairWithSum(sorted, target)`, taking an array sorted in ascending order and returning the two values that add up to `target` as `[smaller, larger]`, found with one index moving in from each end in a `while` loop, or `null` when no such pair exists. `pairWithSum([1, 2, 4, 7, 11], 9)` gives `[2, 7]`. When several pairs qualify, return the one with the smallest first value; a single value cannot pair with itself.
challenges.firstHint: Start at both ends. Move the left index when the sum is too small, the right when it is too large, and stop when they cross.

challenges.title: Palindrome
challenges.prompt: Write `isPalindrome(text)`, returning true when the string reads the same backwards. Assume plain lowercase letters; an empty string and a single character are both palindromes.
challenges.firstHint: Compare the word to its reversed version.

challenges.title: Positive numbers
challenges.prompt: Write `positives(numbers)`, returning a new array of the values strictly above zero, in order. Zero is not positive, and an array with none gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: A keep-or-drop decision on each value, and the only subtlety is the boundary: zero is not above zero.

challenges.title: Serve the queue
challenges.prompt: Write `serveNext(queue, newcomer)`. The newcomer joins the back of the queue with `push`, then the person at the front is served: remove them with `shift` and return their name. The queue is changed in place. With `queue = ["Ana", "Bo"]`, `serveNext(queue, "Cy")` returns `"Ana"` and leaves `queue` as `["Bo", "Cy"]`; an empty queue serves the newcomer at once.
challenges.firstHint: One method adds at the back and another removes from the front; both change the array you were given, and the removing one hands you what it removed.

challenges.title: Remove a range
challenges.prompt: Write `removeRange(list, start, count)`, removing `count` items in place beginning at index `start` with `splice` and returning the removed items as an array. With `list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, `removeRange(list, 1, 2)` returns `[2, 3]` and leaves `list` as `[1, 4, 5]`. A count of zero removes nothing, and a count past the end stops at the end.
challenges.firstHint: One array method both removes a run of elements in place and hands the removed run back, and its first two arguments are exactly where to start and how many.

challenges.title: Remove by id
challenges.prompt: Write `removeById(items, id)`, removing the first object whose `id` equals the given id from the array in place and returning the removed object, or `null` when no object matches — in which case the array is left untouched. Find the position with `findIndex`, then take the object out with `splice`. With `items = [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }]`, `removeById(items, 2)` returns `{ id: 2 }` and leaves `items` as `[{ id: 1 }]`.
challenges.firstHint: Find the position first, and treat -1 as not found before you splice — splicing at -1 would quietly remove the last element.

challenges.title: Repeat word
challenges.prompt: Write `repeat(word, times)`, returning the word repeated that many times with single spaces between — `repeat(“hi”, 3)` gives `hi hi hi`. Once means no space at all, and zero times gives an empty string.
challenges.firstHint: Build the pieces first and let the joining put the separators between them, rather than adding a space each time and trimming one off the end.

challenges.title: Retry on failure
challenges.prompt: Write `retry(fn, attempts)`, calling the async `fn` until it resolves or the attempt budget runs out. Resolve with the first success; when every attempt fails, reject with the last error rather than the first.
challenges.firstHint: Loop over the attempts and return as soon as one resolves.

challenges.title: Reverse in place
challenges.prompt: Write `reverseInPlace(list)`, reversing the array itself with two indexes that start at the ends and swap their way towards the middle, without `reverse()` or a copy, and returning the same array. `reverseInPlace([1, 2, 3, 4])` gives `[4, 3, 2, 1]`. Odd lengths, a single item and an empty array all work.
challenges.firstHint: Keep one index at each end, swap the two elements they point at, and move both indexes towards the middle until they meet or cross.

challenges.title: Reverse string
challenges.prompt: Write `reverse(text)`, returning the string with its characters in the opposite order. Spaces are characters like any other, and an empty or single-character string comes back unchanged.
challenges.firstHint: Add each letter to the front of a result string.

challenges.title: Rotate by n
challenges.prompt: Write `rotateBy(list, n)`, returning a new array with every element moved `n` places to the right and the ones pushed past the end wrapping round to the front, built with a `for` loop and remainder arithmetic rather than `slice`. `rotateBy([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` gives `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`. A negative `n` rotates left, an `n` beyond the length wraps around, an empty array gives an empty array, and the input is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: Bring the shift into the range zero to length minus one first — the remainder operator plus one extra addition handles negatives — then one loop reads each element from its shifted position.

challenges.title: Rotate once
challenges.prompt: Write `rotateOnce(list)`, moving the first element to the end in place with `shift` and `push`, and returning the list. `rotateOnce([1, 2, 3])` gives `[2, 3, 1]`. An empty list stays empty — watch what `shift` returns there — and a single item stays where it is.
challenges.firstHint: Take the first element off with one method and put it on the end with another — and check what the removing method returns when there is nothing to remove.

challenges.title: Run-length encode
challenges.prompt: Write `runLength(text)`, returning the string with each run of the same character replaced by the run’s length followed by the character, found with one `for` loop that counts while the next character matches. `runLength("aaabccdddd")` gives `"3a1b2c4d"`. Runs are case-sensitive, a single character gives `"1"` plus that character, and an empty string gives an empty string.
challenges.firstHint: Count while the next character is the same as the current one, and write the count and the character out the moment the next one differs — the end of the string counts as differing.

challenges.title: Run tasks in order
challenges.prompt: Write `runSequentially(tasks)`, calling an array of async functions one after another — never in parallel — and resolving with their results in order. Plain return values and an empty array both work.
challenges.firstHint: Await each task inside a loop instead of starting them all at once.

challenges.title: Running totals
challenges.prompt: Write `runningTotals(numbers)`, returning a new array where each position holds the sum of every number up to and including that position, built with `reduce` whose accumulator is the output array. `runningTotals([1, 2, 3, 4])` gives `[1, 3, 6, 10]`. An empty array gives an empty array, and the input is not changed.
challenges.firstHint: The accumulator can be the output array itself: the next total is the last one already in it, or zero when it is still empty, plus the current number.

challenges.title: Short words
challenges.prompt: Write `shortWords(words)`, returning only the words with fewer than five characters. Four characters passes, five does not.
challenges.firstHint: A keep-or-drop decision on each word using its length. Read the boundary carefully: four characters passes and five does not.

challenges.title: Sleep
challenges.prompt: Write `sleep(ms)`, returning a promise that resolves after `ms` milliseconds with no value. A zero wait still resolves.
challenges.firstHint: Wrap setTimeout in a promise and resolve it from the callback.

challenges.title: Sliding window max
challenges.prompt: Write `windowMax(numbers, size)`, returning an array with the largest value of every window of `size` consecutive numbers, from left to right, using an outer `for` loop over the window starts and an inner one that scans each window. `windowMax([1, 3, 2, 5, 4], 3)` gives `[3, 5, 5]`. A window wider than the array gives an empty array, and a window as wide as the array gives a single value.
challenges.firstHint: The outer loop picks where a window starts, and stops when a full window no longer fits; the inner loop walks that window keeping the largest value seen.

challenges.title: Any and all
challenges.prompt: Write `passReport(scores, passMark)`, returning `{ anyPassed, allPassed }`: whether at least one score reaches the pass mark, answered with `some`, and whether every score does, answered with `every`. `passReport([40, 70], 50)` gives `{ anyPassed: true, allPassed: false }`. The pass mark itself passes, and for an empty list `some` says false while `every` says true.
challenges.firstHint: Two questions about the same condition — does at least one score reach the mark, and do they all — and each has an array method that answers with a boolean.

challenges.title: Square numbers
challenges.prompt: Write `squares(numbers)`, returning a new array with every number multiplied by itself. A negative squares to a positive; zero and decimals square normally.
challenges.firstHint: One output for every input, and squaring is just a number multiplied by itself — the same shape as doubling.

challenges.title: Sum array
challenges.prompt: Write `sum(numbers)`, returning the total of every value. An empty array totals 0, and negatives and decimals add up like anything else.
challenges.firstHint: You are collapsing many values into one, so reach for the method built for exactly that — and give it a starting total, or an empty array has no answer to return.

challenges.title: Sum labelled pairs
challenges.prompt: Write `totalOf(pairs, label)`, where `pairs` is an array of `[label, value]` pairs, returning the total of the values whose label matches, destructured straight in the head of a `for…of` loop. `totalOf([["food", 12], ["rent", 500], ["food", 8]], "food")` gives 20. No matching label, or an empty array, gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Each element is a two-item array, and for-of can take it apart into a name and a value right in the loop head, so the body only compares and adds.

challenges.title: Sum mixed values
challenges.prompt: Write `sumMixed(values)`, returning the numeric total of an array that mixes numbers with numeric strings such as `"4"` or `"2.5"`, converting each value with `Number` inside a `for…of` loop before adding it. `sumMixed([1, "2", 3])` gives 6, a number, not `"123"`. An empty array gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Plus with a string on one side glues text together, so convert each value to a number before adding it.

challenges.title: Sum with for
challenges.prompt: Write `addUp(numbers)`, returning the total of every number using a `for` loop with an index rather than `reduce`. `addUp([1, 2, 3])` gives 6. An empty array totals 0, and negatives and decimals add up like anything else.
challenges.firstHint: Keep a running total outside the loop, and let an index walk from zero up to, but not including, the length.

challenges.title: Swap pairs
challenges.prompt: Write `swapPairs(list)`, returning a new array in which every two neighbours have traded places, swapped with array destructuring inside a `for` loop that steps by two over a copy of the list. `swapPairs([1, 2, 3, 4])` gives `[2, 1, 4, 3]`. With an odd length the last item stays where it is, an empty array gives an empty array, and the input is never changed.
challenges.firstHint: Copy the array first, then step through it two at a time and swap each neighbour pair with a one-line array destructuring assignment — no temporary variable needed.

challenges.title: Swap the top
challenges.prompt: Write `swapTop(stack, item)`, replacing the top of a stack in place: remove the last element with `pop`, put `item` in its place with `push`, and return the removed element. With `stack = [1, 2, 3]`, `swapTop(stack, 9)` returns 3 and leaves `stack` as `[1, 2, 9]`. On an empty stack there is nothing to remove, so the item is pushed and `undefined` comes back.
challenges.firstHint: pop takes the last element off and gives it to you, push puts one on, and the order of the two calls decides whether the new item sits under or on top.

challenges.title: Throttle calls
challenges.prompt: Write `throttle(fn, waitMs)`, returning a throttled function with a leading edge: the first call runs immediately, and any call made during the next `waitMs` is dropped rather than replayed later. Two throttled functions keep separate windows.
challenges.firstHint: Remember when the last run happened and compare it with now.

challenges.title: Times table
challenges.prompt: Write `timesTable(size)`, returning a square table as an array of rows, where the cell in row r and column c (both counted from 1) holds r times c, built with one `for` loop nested inside another. `timesTable(3)` gives `[[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [3, 6, 9]]`. `timesTable(0)` gives an empty array.
challenges.firstHint: One loop makes the rows and, inside it, a second loop fills each row cell by cell — build a fresh row array on every pass of the outer loop.

challenges.title: Total price
challenges.prompt: Write `total(items)`, returning the sum of every item’s `price`. An empty array totals 0, and decimal prices add up normally.
challenges.firstHint: The same collapse-to-one-value shape as summing numbers, except the number you are adding is a property of each object.

challenges.title: Unique values
challenges.prompt: Write `unique(values)`, returning a new array with duplicates removed, each value kept at the position it was first seen. It works for strings as well as numbers.
challenges.firstHint: Create a Set, then spread it into an array.

challenges.title: Variadic sum
challenges.prompt: Write `sumAll(...numbers)`, taking any number of arguments through a rest parameter and returning their total from a `for…of` loop over that array. `sumAll(1, 2, 3)` gives 6. With no arguments the total is 0, and an array can be spread into the call: `sumAll(...[4, 5])` gives 9.
challenges.firstHint: A rest parameter gathers however many arguments arrive into one real array, and from there it is an ordinary for-of total.

challenges.title: Word count
challenges.prompt: Write `wordCount(sentence)`, returning how many words the sentence holds. Surrounding whitespace does not count, repeated spaces between words do not create extra ones, and an empty string gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Trim the ends first, then decide what separates one word from the next — and check what happens when two spaces sit next to each other.

challenges.title: Words of a length
challenges.prompt: Write `countWordsOfLength(sentence, length)`, returning how many words in the sentence have exactly that many characters. Words are separated by single spaces; split the sentence and walk the words with `for…of`. `countWordsOfLength("the cat sat on a mat", 3)` gives 4, and an empty sentence gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Split the sentence on spaces first, then walk the words and compare each length with the one you were given.

challenges.title: Zip two lists
challenges.prompt: Write `zip(left, right)`, returning an array of `[left[i], right[i]]` pairs built with one `for` loop whose index reads both arrays at once, stopping at the shorter length. `zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"])` gives `[[1, "a"], [2, "b"], [3, "c"]]`. When one side is empty the result is empty, and neither input is changed.
challenges.firstHint: Decide the number of pairs before looping — the smaller of the two lengths — then one index reads both arrays at once.

challenges.title: Abort a request
challenges.prompt: Fetch the posts in an effect, and abort the request if the component unmounts before it resolves so no state update happens afterwards.
challenges.firstHint: Create the controller inside the effect and call controller.abort() in cleanup.

challenges.title: Accordion
challenges.prompt: Render the three sections declared in the starter, each a header button with a body paragraph. No body shows at first; clicking a header opens that one, and opening a second closes the first — never two bodies at once.
challenges.firstHint: Store the id of the single open section rather than a flag on every one.

challenges.title: Add a todo
challenges.prompt: Render a text input, an Add button and a UL that starts empty. Adding appends the typed text as a new LI and clears the input back to empty, and a second task must not replace the first.
challenges.firstHint: Keep input and todos in separate state. Create a new array when adding.

challenges.title: Color selector
challenges.prompt: Render a select over the colours declared in the starter — Red, Blue and Green — plus a line reading “You have selected: <colour>”. It starts on the first one, and choosing another updates the line immediately.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the selected color in state. Bind value and onChange to the select.

challenges.title: Controlled form
challenges.prompt: Render a form with two inputs — a name and an email — and a submit button. Submitting must not reload the page, and both submitted values then appear on screen. Nothing is shown before the first submit.
challenges.firstHint: Call preventDefault in onSubmit and copy form state into submitted state.

challenges.title: Counter
challenges.prompt: Show a number that starts at 0 and a button that adds one to it. Every click counts: three clicks must show 3, not 1.
challenges.firstHint: Start at 0. Update from the previous count inside the click handler.

challenges.title: Create and append
challenges.prompt: Start with an empty UL and an Add button. Clicking it POSTs a new todo and, once the response arrives, appends the created todo to the list — the list goes from no items to one.
challenges.firstHint: After the request succeeds, update with previous => [...previous, created].

challenges.title: CRUD mini app
challenges.prompt: Fetch the posts and render each as an LI holding its title, an Edit button and a Delete button, plus a form that creates a new one. Creating appends a post carrying the typed title; Edit renames that post to “Edited” in place; Delete removes only that post. Edit and delete are local — no request needed.
challenges.firstHint: Build one operation at a time: GET, render, POST, edit with map, delete with filter.

challenges.title: Data list
challenges.prompt: Render the people already declared in the starter as a UL with one LI each, showing the name and the age. Give every LI a key that identifies the person rather than its position in the array.
challenges.firstHint: Map over data. Return one LI for each person and use a stable value as key.

challenges.title: Debounced search
challenges.prompt: Render an input and show the settled query beneath it. That displayed value updates only 500ms after typing stops, so a quick burst of keystrokes produces one update rather than one per key.
challenges.firstHint: Create a timeout when query changes and clear the previous timeout in cleanup.

challenges.title: Delayed message
challenges.prompt: Show “Waiting…” immediately and “Done!” one second later, using a timeout. Clear that timeout when the component unmounts so it can never fire against a component that is gone.
challenges.firstHint: Return a cleanup function that calls clearTimeout.

challenges.title: Dependent fetch
challenges.prompt: Render a select whose option values are user ids — 1 and 2 are enough. Choosing one fetches that user’s posts and renders them as LI items, and changing the selection fetches again; the two users do not have the same number of posts.
challenges.firstHint: Run the posts effect whenever selectedUserId changes.

challenges.title: Document title
challenges.prompt: Render a count starting at 0 and a button that increments it, and keep document.title in step: it holds 0 on first render, and 1 after one click.
challenges.firstHint: Put count in the effect dependency array.

challenges.title: A cancel is not an error
challenges.prompt: The starter loads `/api/prices` with an `AbortController`, and its Cancel button aborts the request. But every rejection shows "Could not load prices", so a cancel looks like a failure. In the `catch`, check the error's `name`: an `AbortError` shows "Cancelled", and any other error still shows "Could not load prices". Check the name, not the message, which differs from browser to browser.
challenges.firstHint: When a `fetch` is aborted, the promise rejects with an error whose `name` is `"AbortError"`. A network failure rejects with a different error, usually a `TypeError`.

challenges.title: Cancel the reminder
challenges.prompt: Pressing "Remind me" shows "Time to stretch" 300 milliseconds later. Pressing "Cancel" while the reminder is waiting stops it, so the message never appears. Keep the id that `setTimeout` returns in a ref rather than in state, and pass it to `clearTimeout` when Cancel is pressed. Pressing "Remind me" again while a reminder waits starts the wait over, so clear the old timeout first. Cancel with nothing waiting does nothing.
challenges.firstHint: `setTimeout` returns an id, and `clearTimeout(id)` stops that timeout if it has not fired yet. A ref keeps the id between renders without causing a render of its own; `clearTimeout(null)` is allowed and does nothing.

challenges.title: Countdown to launch
challenges.prompt: Show a number that starts at 3 and goes down by one every 100 milliseconds. At 0, show "Liftoff!" instead of the number and stop counting: clear the interval then, so it does not keep running. Start the interval with `setInterval` in an effect, and return a cleanup that calls `clearInterval`, so a countdown that leaves the page stops too.
challenges.firstHint: An effect that depends on `count` runs again after every tick. Its cleanup clears the old interval before the next run starts, and once `count` is 0 the effect can return early without starting a new one.

challenges.title: An accessible disclosure
challenges.prompt: The "Shipping details" toggle is a clickable `div`, which a keyboard cannot reach and a screen reader does not announce as a control. Make it a `<button type="button">` with `aria-expanded`, "true" while the details show and "false" while they are hidden. Give the details paragraph an id made with `useId`, so two of these on one page never share it, and point the button's `aria-controls` at that id. Render the details only while they are open.
challenges.firstHint: A real `<button>` is focusable and answers Enter and Space by itself. React writes `aria-expanded={open}` as "true" or "false", which is what the attribute expects.

challenges.title: Draw a card
challenges.prompt: Each card in the deck is a button. Clicking one takes that card out of the deck and shows "You drew <name>". Copy the deck, call `splice(index, 1)` on the copy, and read the drawn card from the array `splice` returns. Never splice the array that is in state, or the `cards` prop App was given. A deck can hold two cards with the same name (each has its own id), and only the one clicked goes.
challenges.firstHint: `splice` changes the array it is called on and returns an array of what it removed. Called on a copy made with spread, it leaves the original alone.

challenges.title: Focus the search box
challenges.prompt: The page has a Name field, a Search field and a "Jump to search" button. Clicking the button puts the keyboard focus in the Search field, so the user can type straight away. Create a ref with `useRef(null)`, attach it to the Search input with the `ref` attribute, and call `focus()` on `ref.current` in the click handler. Nothing is focused before the click, so do not use `autoFocus`.
challenges.firstHint: A ref object keeps the same `current` value between renders. React puts the DOM element into `ref.current` once the input is on the page, and the element has a `focus()` method.

challenges.title: Insert at a position
challenges.prompt: The form has a Name field and a Position field, where 1 is the top of the queue. "Add" inserts the name at that position: copy the queue and call `splice(position - 1, 0, name)` on the copy. A position past the end adds the name at the end, which `splice` does by itself. A position below 1 puts the name at the top: a negative start would make `splice` count from the end.
challenges.firstHint: `splice(start, 0, item)` removes nothing and inserts `item` before the element at `start`. A `start` past the end appends, and a negative `start` counts back from the end.

challenges.title: A field that explains its error
challenges.prompt: The email field has no label, and its error is red text that nothing connects to the field. Replace the "Email" span with a `<label>` whose `htmlFor` matches the input's `id`. When Save is pressed with the field empty, show "Enter your email" in an element with its own id, set `aria-invalid="true"` on the input, and point the input's `aria-describedby` at the error. While there is no error, the input carries neither attribute.
challenges.firstHint: `htmlFor` is how JSX writes the `for` attribute. An attribute whose value is `undefined` is left out, so `error ? "email-error" : undefined` adds `aria-describedby` only while the error shows.

challenges.title: Only the latest search
challenges.prompt: Each change of the query starts a request for `/api/posts?q=<query>`, which answers with matching posts, but an old, slow answer can still arrive last and replace the results of a newer query. Give each run of the effect its own `AbortController`, pass its `signal` to `fetch`, and abort it in the effect's cleanup. React runs that cleanup before the next run and when the component leaves the page, so every request but the latest is cancelled. Ignore the `AbortError` an aborted request rejects with.
challenges.firstHint: The cleanup a run of an effect returns belongs to that run, so it aborts that run's controller, the one the closure remembers. A later run makes a new controller.

challenges.title: Nearest provider wins
challenges.prompt: Create and export `SizeContext` with `createContext("medium")`. `Label` shows its text and then, in brackets, the size it reads from `SizeContext`, like "Page (medium)". In App, wrap the section in a provider with the value "large", and the aside inside it in a provider with the value "small". A Label with no provider above it gets the default; every other Label gets the value of the nearest provider above it.
challenges.firstHint: `createContext(defaultValue)` returns an object with a `Provider`. A provider can sit inside another provider of the same context, and a component reads the one closest above it.

challenges.title: Numbered page buttons
challenges.prompt: The list already shows one page of `songs`. Add a button for each page, labelled 1, 2, 3 and so on up to `Math.ceil(songs.length / PAGE_SIZE)`, inside `<nav aria-label="Pages">`. Clicking a number shows that page. The button of the current page carries `aria-current="page"`, and the others carry no `aria-current` at all, so a screen reader says which page is open. App takes the songs as a prop, so work the page count out from them.
challenges.firstHint: React leaves an attribute out when its value is `undefined`, so `aria-current={number === page ? "page" : undefined}` marks one button and leaves the rest bare.

challenges.title: One page at a time
challenges.prompt: The Previous and Next buttons already change `page`, which starts at 1, but the list shows every photo. Show only the current page: take `photos.slice(start, start + PAGE_SIZE)`, where `start` is `(page - 1) * PAGE_SIZE`, and render each photo as a list item. Under the list, show "Page <page> of <pageCount>". App takes the photos as a prop, so a longer or shorter list pages the same way.
challenges.firstHint: Pages count from 1 and array indexes from 0, so page 1 starts at index 0 and page 2 at index `PAGE_SIZE`. `slice(start, end)` stops before `end` and never runs past the end of the array.

challenges.title: Read the theme
challenges.prompt: `Badge` expects a `theme` prop, but `Toolbar` renders it without one, so it shows "Theme: " and nothing after it. App already provides "dark" through `ThemeContext`. Make `Badge` read the theme with `useContext(ThemeContext)` instead of taking a prop, for both its text and its class name. Leave `Toolbar` as it is: with context, the components in between pass nothing along.
challenges.firstHint: `useContext(SomeContext)` returns the `value` of the nearest `SomeContext.Provider` above the component, or the default passed to `createContext` when there is none.

challenges.title: Share a count through context
challenges.prompt: The basket count lives in App's state. Provide `{ count, add }` through `BasketContext`, where `add` adds one to the count. `AddButton` calls `add` when clicked, and `BasketCount` shows "Items in basket: <count>". Neither takes a prop for this: both read the context with `useContext`. The count starts at 0.
challenges.firstHint: A provider's `value` can be an object that holds both a value and a function that changes it. Every component below the provider that reads the context gets the new value when the state in App changes.

challenges.title: Show more
challenges.prompt: Show the first 3 comments as list items and a "Show more" button under them. Each click shows 3 more. Keep how many are shown in state, not a second copy of the comments, and render `comments.slice(0, shown)`. While any comment is still hidden the button stays; once every comment shows, the button goes away. App takes the comments as a prop, and a short list may need no button at all.
challenges.firstHint: Store a number, the count of comments on screen, and derive the list from it with `slice(0, shown)`. Asking `slice` for more than the array holds is fine: it stops at the end.

challenges.title: Stop the download
challenges.prompt: "Download" fetches `/api/report`, shows "Downloading…" and then "Done" when the response arrives. Make "Stop" cancel it: create a new `AbortController` each time a download starts, keep it in a ref, pass its `signal` to `fetch`, and call `abort()` on it from Stop. The aborted `fetch` rejects, and the code in the starter then shows "Stopped". Stop after a finished download changes nothing, and so does Stop with no download at all.
challenges.firstHint: An `AbortController` cancels once: after `abort()` its signal stays aborted, and a `fetch` given that signal rejects at once. So each download needs a controller of its own, and the ref holds the latest one.

challenges.title: Take a seat
challenges.prompt: A row of four seats holds a name or `null` for a free seat. A free seat shows a "Take seat <n>" button. Clicking it puts "You" in that seat: copy the row and call `splice(index, 1, "You")` on the copy, which replaces one element, so the row keeps four seats and every other seat stays where it was. Once you are seated, the buttons of the other free seats are disabled.
challenges.firstHint: `splice(index, 1, item)` removes one element and puts `item` in its place, so the length does not change.

challenges.title: Totals from a hook
challenges.prompt: Write and export `useBasketTotals(items)`. It returns `{ count, total }`: `count` adds up every item's `quantity`, and `total` adds up `price * quantity`. Work both out from `items` while rendering: no state and no effect inside the hook, so the totals can never fall behind the items. App keeps the items in state, shows "Items: <count>" and "Total: <total>", and its "Add a pen" button appends `{ name: "Pen", price: 2, quantity: 1 }`.
challenges.firstHint: A value you can work out from props or state is not state of its own. Compute it in the body of the hook, and it is fresh on every render.

challenges.title: A useToggle hook
challenges.prompt: Write and export `useToggle(initial = false)`, a hook that keeps a boolean in state and returns `[on, toggle]`, where `toggle` flips it. Use it twice in App: Wi-Fi starts on and Bluetooth starts off. Each button reads "Wi-Fi: on" or "Wi-Fi: off" (and the same for Bluetooth) and flips only its own setting. Two calls to one hook share the code, never the state.
challenges.firstHint: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks. Each component call gets its own state, just as two `useState` calls do.

challenges.title: A useWindowWidth hook
challenges.prompt: Write and export `useWindowWidth()`. It starts from `window.innerWidth` and returns the current width. In an effect that runs once, add a `resize` listener on `window` that stores the new width, and in the effect's cleanup remove that same listener: `removeEventListener` only removes a listener it is given the very same function for. App shows "Width: <n>px".
challenges.firstHint: Name the listener once inside the effect, then pass that one function to both `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener`. An inline arrow in the cleanup is a new function, so nothing would be removed.

challenges.title: Breadcrumbs from a path
challenges.prompt: Show the current `path` as breadcrumbs. For "/docs/react/hooks" the crumbs read "docs", "react" and "hooks". Every crumb but the last is a link to the path up to and including it, "/docs" and then "/docs/react", and the last is plain text. Split the path on "/", drop the empty parts that the leading slash and any trailing slash leave, and build each link from `parts.slice(0, index + 1)`. Work the crumbs out while rendering, so they follow when "Go up" shortens the path.
challenges.firstHint: `"/docs/react".split("/")` gives `["", "docs", "react"]`: the leading slash leaves an empty string in front. `slice(0, n)` copies the first `n` parts, so the crumb at `index` needs `index + 1` of them.

challenges.title: Characters left
challenges.prompt: A post holds at most 80 characters. Under the text box, show "Characters left: <n>", or "Too long by <n>" once the text runs over. Disable Post while the text is empty or too long. Work all of it out from `text` while rendering: a count kept in a state of its own needs an update on every change, and one missed update leaves it wrong.
challenges.firstHint: Anything you can work out from state during render is not state itself. `LIMIT - text.length` is right for whatever text is on screen, so there is nothing to keep in step.

challenges.title: Dispatch through context
challenges.prompt: App keeps the tasks in a reducer and hands `dispatch` to `AddTask` and, through `TaskList`, to every `TaskItem` as an `onDispatch` prop. `TaskList` never uses it; it only passes it on. Provide `dispatch` through `TasksDispatchContext` around the page instead, have `AddTask` and `TaskItem` read it with `useContext`, and remove the `onDispatch` props.
challenges.firstHint: The `dispatch` that `useReducer` returns stays the same function for the whole life of the component, so it makes a steady context value: the components that read it never re-render because it changed.

challenges.title: Ask the server for one page
challenges.prompt: The server hands out posts one page at a time. Whenever `page` changes, fetch `/api/posts?_page=<page>&_limit=5` in an effect and show the titles it sends back. The server never says how many pages there are, so a page that comes back with fewer than 5 posts is the last one: disable Next then. Disable Previous on page 1.
challenges.firstHint: An effect with `[page]` as its dependency array runs after the first render and again after every render in which `page` changed. That is the moment to ask for the new page.

challenges.title: Give the focus back
challenges.prompt: "Rename" opens a small form, and its field takes the keyboard focus. When the form closes, by Save, by Cancel or by the Escape key, the field leaves the page and the focus drops to the page body, so a keyboard user has to find their place again. Put a ref on the Rename button and call `focus()` on it whenever the form closes. Escape anywhere in the form closes it without saving.
challenges.firstHint: When the element that has the focus leaves the page, the browser moves the focus to the `body`. The Rename button stays on the page the whole time, so the handler that closes the form can focus it straight away.

challenges.title: Remove listeners with one abort
challenges.prompt: The status line shows which device you used last: "Last input: keyboard" after a key press anywhere in the window, and "Last input: mouse" after the mouse moves. Add both listeners to `window` in one effect that runs once, and give each of them the options `{ signal: controller.signal }` from a single `AbortController`. The effect's cleanup is then one call, `controller.abort()`, which removes both listeners without a `removeEventListener` for each.
challenges.firstHint: `addEventListener` takes an options object as its third argument. A listener added with a `signal` goes away when that signal aborts, and any number of listeners can share one signal.

challenges.title: Name the remove buttons
challenges.prompt: Each song in the playlist has a "×" button, and a screen reader reads every one of them the same way, so nobody can tell which song a button removes. Give each button an `aria-label` of "Remove <title>"; the "×" stays as the text you see. Make the button remove its song: copy the playlist and call `splice(index, 1)` on the copy. Remove by position, because the same song can be on the list twice.
challenges.firstHint: A screen reader reads a button by its accessible name. By default that is the text inside it; `aria-label` replaces it, and the "×" still shows on screen.

challenges.title: One Stop for two requests
challenges.prompt: "Load" asks for a user and their posts at once, `/api/users/1` and `/api/posts?userId=1`, and shows "Leanne Graham, 3 posts" when both arrive. "Stop" should cancel both. Create one `AbortController` for each load, keep it in a ref, pass the same `signal` to both `fetch` calls, and call `abort()` from Stop: one signal cancels every request that carries it. Show "Stopped" when the error is an `AbortError`, and keep "Could not load" for anything else.
challenges.firstHint: A signal belongs to its controller, not to one request. Every `fetch` given the same signal rejects when that controller aborts, and `Promise.all` rejects as soon as the first of them does.

challenges.title: Buttons that say they are pressed
challenges.prompt: Bold and Italic should switch their style on and off for the preview line, and a pressed button should say so. Give each button a state of its own and a click that flips it. Show that state with `aria-pressed`: `true` while the style is on and `false` while it is off. A screen reader announces the attribute as "pressed" or "not pressed", which a change of color cannot tell anyone. Keep the labels "Bold" and "Italic" as they are.
challenges.firstHint: React writes `aria-pressed={true}` as "true" and `aria-pressed={false}` as "false", the two values the attribute expects. To a screen reader, a button with `aria-pressed` is a toggle button.

challenges.title: A radio group through context
challenges.prompt: `RadioGroup` takes a `name`, the chosen `value` and an `onChange`, and every `Radio` inside it needs all three. Have `RadioGroup` provide `{ name, value, onChange }` through `RadioContext`, and have `Radio` read it with `useContext`. Each Radio's input takes the group's `name`, is `checked` when its own `value` equals the group's, and calls `onChange` with its own value when picked. App passes each Radio only its value and its label.
challenges.firstHint: A component can provide context to its own `children`. The Radio elements App passes in render inside RadioGroup's provider, so each one reads the group around it, and none of them needs the settings as props.

challenges.title: Read more
challenges.prompt: A review longer than 60 characters starts folded: show `text.slice(0, 60)` followed by "...", with a "Read more" button under it. The button shows the whole review and turns into "Show less", which folds it again. A review of 60 characters or fewer shows in full, with no button at all.
challenges.firstHint: `slice(0, n)` on a string returns its first `n` characters and leaves the string as it was. A button that should not exist stays out of the JSX: `{long && <button>...</button>}` renders nothing when `long` is false.

challenges.title: The results line
challenges.prompt: Under the recipes, a line says which ones the page shows: "Showing 1 to 4 of 10 recipes" on the first page. Work both ends out from `page` while rendering. The first is `(page - 1) * PAGE_SIZE + 1`, and the last is `page * PAGE_SIZE`, but never more than the number of recipes. With no recipes at all, the line reads "No recipes". Disable Previous on the first page and Next on the last, and both when there are no recipes. `page` stays the only state.
challenges.firstHint: People count results from 1 and arrays count from 0, so the first recipe on a page sits at index `start` and reads as number `start + 1`. `Math.min(a, b)` keeps the smaller of two numbers, which trims the last page.

challenges.title: Rows per page
challenges.prompt: The list shows 23 orders one page at a time, and a "Rows per page" select offers 5, 10 and 20. Show the orders of the current page with `orders.slice(start, start + rowsPerPage)`, where `start` is `(page - 1) * rowsPerPage`. When the reader picks another size, go back to page 1: page 4 of five rows would point past the end once a page holds twenty. A select hands you its value as text, so turn it into a number before you store it.
challenges.firstHint: Page 1 starts at index 0 and page 2 at index `rowsPerPage`. `slice` stops before its end index and never runs past the end of the array, so a short last page needs no special case.

challenges.title: Send the latest draft
challenges.prompt: "Send later" sends the message 300 milliseconds after the click and shows "Sent: <text>". Whatever you type during that wait belongs in the message, but the timeout reads `draft` from the render in which you clicked, so it sends the old text. Keep the latest draft in a ref as well: set `draftRef.current` in the change handler, and read `draftRef.current` when the timeout fires. If the field is empty by then, nothing is sent.
challenges.firstHint: Each render makes new handler functions, and each one sees the state of its own render. A timeout keeps the function it was given, so it keeps that render's `draft`. A ref is one object shared by every render, so `ref.current` read later gives the value written last.

challenges.title: Give up on a slow request
challenges.prompt: "Load" fetches `/api/users/1` and greets the user by name. When the server takes longer than 300 milliseconds, give up. Create an `AbortController` for each load, pass its `signal` to `fetch`, and start a `setTimeout` that calls `abort()` after 300 milliseconds. The aborted request rejects with an `AbortError`: show "The server is taking too long" for it, and keep "Could not load the user" for any other error. Clear the timeout once the request has finished, so a load that answered in time is never aborted afterwards.
challenges.firstHint: A timeout and an `AbortController` work as a pair: the timeout calls `controller.abort()`, and the `fetch` that got `controller.signal` rejects at once with an error named "AbortError". `clearTimeout` stops a timeout that has not fired yet.

challenges.title: Split a line in place
challenges.prompt: Some lines on the shopping list hold more than one thing, such as "Eggs and milk". Every line that contains " and " has a Split button, which replaces the line with its parts in the same place: "Eggs", then "milk". Get the parts with `split(" and ")`, copy the list, and call `splice(index, 1, ...parts)` on the copy. That one call removes the line and inserts every part where it stood.
challenges.firstHint: `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` removes `deleteCount` elements and inserts every item in their place, in order. Spread the parts into the call; passed as one array, they would go in as a single element.

challenges.title: Undo a removal
challenges.prompt: Removing a task shows an "Undo" button. Undo puts the task back at the position it came from, and the button goes away. When a task is removed, remember it and its index in state. For Undo, copy the list and call `splice(index, 0, task)` on the copy, which inserts without removing anything. Only the latest removal can be undone.
challenges.firstHint: `splice(index, 0, item)` removes nothing and inserts `item` before the element now at `index`. An index equal to the length inserts at the end, which is where a removed last task came from.

challenges.title: A useInterval hook
challenges.prompt: Write and export `useInterval(callback, delay)`. It calls `callback` every `delay` milliseconds, and a `delay` of `null` runs no interval, which is how a caller pauses it. Start the interval in an effect that depends on `delay` alone, and clear it in the cleanup. Keep the latest `callback` in a ref, updated in an effect of its own, and call `ref.current()` on each tick: a new callback on every render then never restarts the timer. App counts up every 100 milliseconds, and Pause stops the count.
challenges.firstHint: An effect whose dependencies change runs its cleanup and starts again. If the interval effect depended on `callback`, the new function from each render would clear the timer and start it over, and a component that renders more often than `delay` would never see a tick.

challenges.title: A useOutsideClick hook
challenges.prompt: "Filters" opens a panel of options, and a press anywhere outside should close it. Write and export `useOutsideClick(ref, onOutside)`. In an effect, listen for `mousedown` on `document` and call `onOutside` when `ref.current` does not contain the event's `target`; remove the same listener in the effect's cleanup. In App, put a ref on the `div` that holds both the button and the panel. A press on Filters then counts as inside, and the button can still close the panel itself.
challenges.firstHint: `element.contains(node)` is true for the element itself and for anything inside it. A custom hook can take a ref from the component that calls it, and that ref tells the hook which element counts as inside.

challenges.title: A useTheme hook with a guard
challenges.prompt: `Badge` reads the theme with `useContext(ThemeContext)`. Rendered outside `ThemeProvider`, it gets `null` and shows "Theme: " with nothing after it, and nothing says why. Write and export `useTheme()`. It reads `ThemeContext`, throws `new Error("useTheme must be used inside ThemeProvider")` when the value is `null`, and returns the value otherwise. Use it in `Badge` in place of `useContext`.
challenges.firstHint: `useContext` returns the default from `createContext` when no provider sits above the component. Here the default is `null`, so a `null` value means the component was rendered in the wrong place. A hook may throw during render, and its message can name the mistake.

challenges.title: Effect on mount
challenges.prompt: Render the text “Waiting…” and replace it with “Ready!” once the component has mounted — after the first render, not during it. The waiting text must be gone afterwards.
challenges.firstHint: An effect with [] runs after the first render.

challenges.title: Fetch error state
