challenges.prompt: Fetch the users list and render one LI per user. When the request fails, render no list items at all and show a short message instead — and treat a non-OK response as a failure, not only a thrown network error.
challenges.firstHint: Check response.ok and throw an Error before reading JSON.

challenges.title: Filter fetched users
challenges.prompt: Fetch the users once, then filter the rendered LI list with a text input, ignoring case. The filtering happens locally: do not send a new request on every keystroke.
challenges.firstHint: Fetch once. Filter locally from users and query—do not fetch on every keystroke.

challenges.title: GET one user
challenges.prompt: Fetch user 1 from the training API and render that user’s name and email once the response arrives.
challenges.firstHint: Fetch in an effect, await response.json(), then save the user in state.

challenges.title: GET users list
challenges.prompt: Fetch the users list and render one LI per user showing their name. Start from an empty array so the first render, before any data arrives, does not throw.
challenges.firstHint: Start with an empty array so users.map is always safe.

challenges.title: Greeting component
challenges.prompt: Write a `Greeting` component that takes a `name` prop and renders a paragraph reading “Hello, <name>”. In `App`, map over the `names` array declared in the starter and render one `Greeting` per name, so the page shows three paragraphs, “Hello, Ana”, “Hello, Bo” and “Hello, Cyril”, in that order.
challenges.firstHint: A component is a function that receives props and returns JSX, and map can return one of them per array element.

challenges.title: Guest list
challenges.prompt: Start from the `initialGuests` declared in the starter and render a text input, an Add button and a UL with one LI per guest holding the name and its own Remove button. Add appends the typed name to the end of the list and clears the input; Remove drops only that guest. Never mutate an existing array: build a new one with spread when adding and with `filter` when removing, so a fresh mount still starts from the two original guests.
challenges.firstHint: Both updates produce a new array: spread the old one plus the new guest, or filter the old one by id.

challenges.title: Heading and intro
challenges.prompt: The starter declares two constants, `title` and `intro`. Render `title` inside an h1 and `intro` inside a paragraph, placing the constants in the JSX instead of retyping their text. The page must show exactly “Deep End” as its h1 and “Practise React one list at a time.” as its paragraph.
challenges.firstHint: Curly braces let you drop a JavaScript value into JSX markup.

challenges.title: In-stock list
challenges.prompt: Render only the `products` declared in the starter whose `inStock` is true, as a UL with one LI per product name, plus a paragraph reading “2 of 4 in stock”. Filter the array before mapping it, so Snorkel and Wetsuit never appear, and key each LI by the product id.
challenges.firstHint: Chain filter and map: filter keeps the products you want and map turns each one into a list item.

challenges.title: Insert and reorder
challenges.prompt: Render `initialStops` as an OL. Each LI shows the stop name in a span and three buttons: “Insert after”, “Up”, and “Down”. Insert a new “Stop <n>”, using the next length, directly after the selected item. Up and Down swap with a neighbour and do nothing at the edges. Build new arrays with `slice` and spread; never mutate the previous state. Inserting after Reef should give Harbour, Reef, Stop 4, Lighthouse.
challenges.firstHint: Cut the array into the part before the position and the part after it, then spread both around whatever belongs in between.

challenges.title: Keyed book list
challenges.prompt: Render the `books` declared in the starter as a UL with one LI per book reading “<title> by <author>” in array order, for example “Dune by Frank Herbert”, with a paragraph above it reading “3 books”. Each LI takes its key from the book's `id`, never from the array index.
challenges.firstHint: One map call over the array returns every list item, and the key goes on the element the callback returns.

challenges.title: Live paragraph
challenges.prompt: Render a text input and a paragraph under it. The paragraph shows exactly what the input currently holds, updating on every keystroke, and the input stays controlled — its value comes from your state.
challenges.firstHint: Use one state value for both the input value and paragraph text.

challenges.title: Loading state
challenges.prompt: Fetch the users list. Show “Loading…” while the request is in flight, then replace it with one LI per user showing their name.
challenges.firstHint: Set loading false in finally so success and failure both finish loading.

challenges.title: Memoised total
challenges.prompt: Render a search input, a UL of the `orders` declared in the starter whose name contains the query ignoring case, and a paragraph reading “Total: <sum of the matching prices>”, so an empty query shows all six with “Total: 585” and “dive” shows two with “Total: 180”. Add a button labelled “Nudge” that increments a counter shown as “Nudges: <n>”. Compute the filtered list and its total inside one `useMemo` that depends only on the query, so a re-render caused by Nudge skips that work.
challenges.firstHint: useMemo takes a function that returns the filtered list with its total, and a dependency array holding the query alone.

challenges.title: Modal
challenges.prompt: An Open button shows an element with role="dialog" inside a backdrop. It closes on the Close button, on the Escape key, and on a click on the backdrop — but a click inside the dialog itself must leave it open.
challenges.firstHint: Add the key listener in an effect while the dialog is open and remove it in the cleanup.

challenges.title: Newest-first todos
challenges.prompt: Render a form with a text input and an Add button, and a UL that starts empty. Submitting adds the trimmed text as a new LI at the top of the list, above everything added earlier, and clears the input; a blank submission adds nothing. Adding “First” and then “Second” must list Second before First.
challenges.firstHint: Put the new item first and spread the previous array after it, which is the immutable form of unshift.

challenges.title: Optimistic todo
challenges.prompt: Render a form with a title input. On submit, add the todo to the list straight away — before the POST resolves — then send it. If the request fails, take it back out so the list returns to empty.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the previous list so catch can restore it if the request fails.

challenges.title: Paginated posts
challenges.prompt: Fetch the posts and show five at a time as LI items, with Previous and Next buttons. The first page holds posts one to five; Next moves to the following five.
challenges.firstHint: Keep page in state. Calculate start index, then slice the fetched array.

challenges.title: POST a new post
challenges.prompt: Render a form with a title input. On submit, POST that title as JSON to the posts endpoint and render what comes back — the title, and the id the API assigns it.
challenges.firstHint: Use method POST, a JSON content-type header, and JSON.stringify for the body.

challenges.title: Price component
challenges.prompt: Write a `Price` component that takes `amount` and `currency` props and renders a span with the amount to two decimals, a space and the currency, so `amount={3.5}` with `currency="EUR"` gives “3.50 EUR”. Render the `items` declared in the starter as a UL with one LI per item holding the item name and its `Price`, keyed by the item id.
challenges.firstHint: Props arrive as a single object argument, and toFixed(2) turns a number into a two-decimal string.

challenges.title: Product search
challenges.prompt: Fetch the products from the training API on mount — this endpoint nests its array under a products key, so the array is not the response body itself. Each LI shows three fields from the product: its title, its price and its category. A search input filters as you type, matching case-insensitively against the title or the category, so “tech” finds the laptop. Above the list a line reads “Total: n”, the summed price of only the products currently shown.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the fetched list and the search text in separate state, and work out what is shown from both during render rather than storing a second list.

challenges.title: Refresh data
challenges.prompt: Fetch one todo when the component mounts and render its title, and fetch another when a Refresh button is clicked. Put the request in a single function that both the effect and the click handler call.
challenges.firstHint: Put the request in a function that both useEffect and onClick can call.

challenges.title: Remove a todo
challenges.prompt: The starter holds three todos. Render each as an LI with its text and its own Remove button; clicking one Remove deletes only that todo and leaves the others in place.
challenges.firstHint: Filter out the item whose id matches the clicked button.

challenges.title: Reorder with stable keys
challenges.prompt: Render `initialSteps` as an OL. Each LI shows the label plus Up and Down buttons; disable Up on the first item and Down on the last. For a move, copy the array, remove the item with `splice`, insert it one position over with another `splice`, and store the copy. Key each LI by the step’s `id`. Moving Build down should produce Plan, Test, Build, Ship while preserving the same LI element.
challenges.firstHint: One splice removes the item at its index and hands it back, and a second splice inserts it at the neighbouring index in the same copy.

challenges.title: Reusable useFetch hook
challenges.prompt: Write useFetch(url) returning data, loading and error, and use it in App: “Loading…” while the request is in flight, one LI per user on success, and no list items plus a message when it fails.
challenges.firstHint: Move the three state values and request effect into a function whose name starts with use.

challenges.title: Search a list
challenges.prompt: Filter the names declared in the starter with a text input, rendering the matches as LI items — all three before anything is typed. Matching ignores case, so typing ANA still leaves Ana on screen.
challenges.firstHint: Store only the query. Derive filtered names during render.

challenges.title: Select fetched user
challenges.prompt: Fetch the users and render one button per user, labelled with their name. Their details — name and email — appear only after a button is clicked; nothing is selected at first.
challenges.firstHint: Keep users and selectedUser in separate state values.

challenges.title: Show and hide
challenges.prompt: Render a button and a paragraph. The paragraph must not be in the DOM at first; clicking adds it, clicking again removes it. Render it conditionally rather than hiding it with CSS.
challenges.firstHint: Render the paragraph only when a boolean state value is true.

challenges.title: Stable pick handler
challenges.prompt: Render a paragraph reading “Picked: none” and one button per flavour declared in the starter, each rendered by a `FlavourButton` child wrapped in `React.memo` that receives `label` and `onPick` props. Clicking a button passes its label to `onPick` and the paragraph shows it, so clicking Mint gives “Picked: Mint”. Create `onPick` with `useCallback` and an empty dependency array, so the memoised children receive the same function on every render.
challenges.firstHint: A function created in the component body is new on every render, while useCallback with no dependencies hands back the same one each time.

challenges.title: Star rating
challenges.prompt: Render one button per entry in the stars array from the starter, plus a line reading “Rating: n” starting at 0. Hovering a star previews that rating, moving the pointer away restores the committed one, and clicking commits it — after clicking the fourth star the line reads “Rating: 4”.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the hovered value and the committed value apart, and display whichever applies.

challenges.title: Stopwatch
challenges.prompt: Show elapsed whole seconds in a paragraph, starting at 0, with Start, Stop and Reset buttons. Start counts up once a second, Stop freezes the number where it is, and Reset returns it to 0. Pressing Start twice must not leave two intervals running.
challenges.firstHint: Keep the interval id in a ref so Stop can clear the interval Start created.

challenges.title: Tabs
challenges.prompt: Render the three tabs declared in the starter, each a button with role="tab", and exactly one element with role="tabpanel" holding the selected tab’s content. The selected tab carries aria-selected="true" and the others "false".
challenges.firstHint: Store the active tab id, and give the tabs role tab with aria-selected.

challenges.title: Theme context
challenges.prompt: Create a theme context holding “light” or “dark” plus a way to change it. App provides it; a nested child — not App itself — reads the value and renders a button that shows the current theme and switches it on click.
challenges.firstHint: Put the value and its setter in one provider value so any depth can reach both.

challenges.title: Ticket queue
challenges.prompt: Render a “Take a ticket” button, a “Call next” button, a paragraph reading “Next up: <first ticket or none>”, a paragraph reading “Waiting: <n>” and a UL of the waiting tickets in order. Keep the queue in `useReducer`: an `enqueue` action appends “Ticket <n>” with n counting up from 1 for the whole session, and a `dequeue` action removes the first ticket. Call next is disabled when nobody waits, so three takes and one call leave Ticket 2 and Ticket 3 with “Next up: Ticket 2”.
challenges.firstHint: Keep both the waiting list and the number of tickets issued in the reducer state, and copy the list before calling shift on it.

challenges.title: Todo dashboard
challenges.prompt: Fetch the first three todos from the training API on mount. Each todo in the response carries a title and a completed flag, and each LI has to show both: the title, then “done” or “to do”, then a Remove button. Above the list show a line reading “Done: n of m”, where n counts the completed ones. A text input and an Add button append a new todo with that title and completed false, and Remove drops that one todo.
challenges.firstHint: One state array holds the todos, whichever way they arrived. Adding, removing and counting are all derivations of it.

challenges.title: Toggle button
challenges.prompt: Render one button whose own label reads OFF to start with, flips to ON when clicked, and back to OFF when clicked again. The word lives inside the button, not beside it.
challenges.firstHint: Store a boolean and replace it with its opposite on click.

challenges.title: Toggle done with map
challenges.prompt: Render the `initialTasks` declared in the starter as a UL where every LI holds a checkbox followed by the task text, checked when `done` is true, plus a paragraph reading “1 of 3 done”. Clicking a checkbox flips only that task's `done` and keeps the list order, so ticking “Write tests” makes the paragraph read “2 of 3 done”. Update with `map`, returning a new object for the matching task and the same object for every other one, so a fresh mount starts again from the seed.
challenges.firstHint: Map over the previous array and spread the matching task into a copy with done flipped, leaving every other task as it was.

challenges.title: Undo stack
challenges.prompt: Render a Push button, an Undo button, a paragraph reading “Depth: <n>” and a UL listing the stack from bottom to top. Manage the stack with `useReducer`: a `push` action adds “Step <n>” where n is the new depth, and a `pop` action removes the last entry. Undo is disabled while the stack is empty, so two pushes and one undo leave only “Step 1” with “Depth: 1”.
challenges.firstHint: Inside the reducer, copy the array before calling push or pop on it, then return the copy.

challenges.title: useDebounce hook
challenges.prompt: Write useDebounce(value, delay), returning the value only once it has stopped changing for delay. Use it to filter the fruits declared in the starter into a UL: all three show at first, and typing narrows the list only after typing settles.
challenges.firstHint: Every new value schedules a timeout, and the cleanup cancels the previous one.

challenges.title: useLocalStorage hook
challenges.prompt: Write useLocalStorage(key, initial), which behaves like useState but persists. Use it for a counter rendered as “Count: n” with an Increment button: it starts from initial when storage is empty, writes every change to localStorage, and reads the count back after a remount.
challenges.firstHint: Read the stored value when state is first created and write it back whenever it changes.

challenges.title: usePagination hook
challenges.prompt: Write `usePagination(items, pageSize)`, a hook that keeps the current page in state and returns that page's items, the page number, the page count and functions that move forward and back. Use it in App with the `cities` declared in the starter and a page size of 3: render the page items as a UL, a paragraph reading “Page 1 of 3”, and Previous and Next buttons that are disabled on the first and the last page. Cut each page out of the array with `slice`.
challenges.firstHint: Multiply the zero-based page index by the page size to find where a page starts, then slice one page length from there.

challenges.title: User by id
challenges.prompt: Render a select whose option values are user ids — 1 and 2 are enough — and fetch that user whenever the selection changes, showing the fetched name. Changing the selection must fetch again rather than keep showing the first user.
challenges.firstHint: Put selectedId in the dependency array and build the URL from it.

challenges.title: Apply a patch
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Settings` with a `theme` string and a `fontSize` number, then write `applyPatch(settings: Settings, patch: Partial<Settings>): Settings`, returning a new settings object with whatever the patch supplies written over the original.
challenges.firstHint: Partial takes a type you already have and makes every property optional, which is exactly what a patch is.

challenges.title: Apply patches in order
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Profile` with a `name` string, an `age` number and a `city` string, then write `applyPatches(profile: Profile, patches: Partial<Profile>[]): Profile`, applying every patch in order and building a new object each time, so the profile handed in is never changed. `applyPatches({ name: "Ada", age: 36, city: "London" }, [{ age: 37 }, { city: "Paris" }])` gives `{ name: "Ada", age: 37, city: "Paris" }`.
challenges.firstHint: Partial<Profile> lets a patch carry any subset of the properties, and spreading it after the current object is what makes the later patch win.

challenges.title: Area of a shape
challenges.prompt: Declare a type alias named `Shape` for a square with a `side`, a rectangle with `width` and `height`, or a triangle with `base` and `height`, each tagged with a `kind`. Then write `area(shape: Shape): number` returning the area of whichever it turns out to be.
challenges.firstHint: Every member of the union carries the same tag with a different exact value, and checking that tag is what unlocks the rest of the object.

challenges.title: Binary search
challenges.prompt: Write `binarySearch(sorted: readonly number[], target: number): number`, returning the index of the target in an ascending list or -1 when it is absent, by halving the search range in a `while` loop: compare the middle value, then continue in the left or the right half. `binarySearch([1, 3, 5, 7], 5)` gives 2, and an empty list gives -1.
challenges.firstHint: Keep a low and a high index that bound the values still worth looking at, and stop once the low index passes the high one.

challenges.title: Chunk a list
challenges.prompt: Write `chunk<T>(items: T[], size: number): T[][]`, splitting a list into groups of `size` items with a `for` loop that steps by `size` and slices out each group; the last group holds whatever is left. `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` gives `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]`, and an empty list gives an empty list. The size is always at least 1.
challenges.firstHint: The loop counter is a start index, and moving it by the group size each pass means every group begins where the previous one ended.

challenges.title: Count a status
challenges.prompt: Declare a string enum `Status` with `Todo = "todo"`, `Doing = "doing"` and `Done = "done"`, then write `countStatus(items: Status[], wanted: Status): number` counting with `reduce` how many items equal the wanted member. `countStatus([Status.Done, Status.Todo, Status.Done], Status.Done)` gives 2, and an empty list gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: The accumulator is a plain number that starts at zero, and each step either adds one or hands it on unchanged.

challenges.title: Describe a value
challenges.prompt: Write `describeValue(value: unknown): string`, returning `nothing` for null or undefined, `a list` for an array, `text` for a string, `a number` for a number, and `something else` for anything left over.
challenges.firstHint: typeof reports null as an object, so ruling out the empty cases first is what stops them taking the wrong branch.

challenges.title: Add a tag to a read-only note
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface `Note` with a `title` string and a list of `tags`, both `readonly`, and type the list as `readonly string[]`, so `note.tags.push(...)` is a compile error. Write `addTag(note: Note, tag: string): Note`, returning a new note whose tags end with `tag`, built with spread for the note and for its tags. When the note already has the tag, return the note unchanged.
challenges.firstHint: Two spreads do it: one copies the note’s properties into a new object, the other copies its tags into a new array with the tag added at the end. `includes` works on a readonly array, because it changes nothing.

challenges.title: Airport codes to names
challenges.prompt: A flight route is written as airport codes joined by dashes, such as `"PRG-LHR-JFK"`. Write `routeNames(route: string, airports: Map<string, string>): string[]`, splitting the route on `-` and looking each code up in the `Map`. The Map’s keys are in capitals, so `"prg"` finds `"PRG"`. A code the Map does not know stays exactly as it was written, and an empty route gives an empty list.
challenges.firstHint: `airports.get(key)` gives the name or `undefined`, and `??` swaps `undefined` for a fallback. `"".split("-")` gives `[""]`, not `[]`, so answer an empty route before you split.

challenges.title: Article previews
challenges.prompt: A news page lists articles as cards that show only the `id` and the `title`. Declare `type Preview = Pick<Article, "id" | "title">`, then write `toPreviews(articles: Article[]): Preview[]`, returning one preview per article in the same order. A preview carries those two properties and nothing else, so the `body` and the `author` stay behind. `Article` is declared for you.
challenges.firstHint: `Pick<Article, "id" | "title">` builds a type with just those two properties. `map` gives one result per article. Build each result from the two properties: returning the whole article would keep the body.

challenges.title: Build a query string
challenges.prompt: Write `toQuery(params: Record<string, string | number>): string`, turning an object into a URL query string such as `"page=2&sort=new"`. Walk `Object.entries(params)` with `for...of`, destructuring each `[key, value]` pair, and encode both with `encodeURIComponent`, so a space becomes `%20` and an `&` inside a value becomes `%26`. Pairs keep the object’s key order, and an empty object gives an empty string.
challenges.firstHint: `Object.entries` gives `[key, value]` pairs you can destructure in the loop head. `encodeURIComponent` takes a number as well as a string. `join("&")` on an empty list gives `""`.

challenges.title: The cheapest offer
challenges.prompt: Write `cheapest<T extends { price: number }>(items: T[]): T | null`, returning the item with the lowest `price`, or `null` for an empty list. Find it with `reduce`. On a tie the first of the equal items wins. Return the item itself, with all its properties, rather than its price.
challenges.firstHint: `reduce` with no starting value begins with the first item as `best`, and throws on an empty array, so check the length first. Swap `best` for `item` only when `item.price` is strictly lower, and the first of two equal prices stays.

challenges.title: A heading for every column
challenges.prompt: A contact table needs a heading for each column. Declare `const LABELS: Record<keyof Contact, string>` holding the headings `Full name`, `Email` and `Phone number`. With that type, leaving out a column, or adding one `Contact` does not have, is a compile error. Then write `headings(columns: (keyof Contact)[]): string[]`, returning the heading of each column in the order asked.
challenges.firstHint: `Record<keyof Contact, string>` is an object type with exactly the keys `name`, `email` and `phone`, each holding a string. `LABELS[column]` is then a string for any column the function accepts.

challenges.title: What the draft still needs
challenges.prompt: A blog editor saves drafts before every field is filled in. `Post` has a `title`, a `body` and a list of `tags`. Write `missingFields(draft: Partial<Post>): string[]`, returning the names of the fields the draft does not have yet, in the order `title`, `body`, `tags`. `Partial<Post>` is `Post` with every property optional, so `{ title: "Hi" }` is a valid draft. A field counts as missing only when it is `undefined`: an empty title is still a title.
challenges.firstHint: `Partial<Post>` gives you a type where `title`, `body` and `tags` may each be absent. List the three field names in an array and `filter` it: keep a name when `draft[name]` is `undefined`.

challenges.title: Fields from the API
challenges.prompt: An API sends each user as `{ user_name: string; avatar_url?: string }`, and the app wants `{ name: string; avatar: string | null }`. Declare the two shapes as `ApiUser` and `Profile`, then write `toProfile(raw: ApiUser): Profile` with one object destructuring that renames both fields and gives a missing avatar the default `null`. An empty `avatar_url` is still a value the API sent, so it stays.
challenges.firstHint: `const { user_name: name } = raw` reads `user_name` into a variable called `name`. Add `= null` after the new name, and the default applies when the property is missing or `undefined`, but not when it is an empty string.

challenges.title: The first error
challenges.prompt: A batch job reports one `Result` per step: `{ ok: true; value: number }` when the step worked and `{ ok: false; error: string }` when it failed. Write `firstError(results: Result[]): string | null`, walking the results with `for...of` and returning the first error message, or `null` when every step worked. `result.error` only compiles after a check on `result.ok` has narrowed the union to the failed shape.
challenges.firstHint: `ok` is the tag of the union. Inside `if (!result.ok)` the compiler knows `result` is `{ ok: false; error: string }`, so `result.error` is a string. Return from inside the loop as soon as you find one.

challenges.title: Flip a pair
challenges.prompt: Write `flip<A, B>([first, second]: [A, B]): [B, A]`, taking a tuple of two items and returning a new tuple with them the other way round. Pull the two items out with array destructuring in the parameter list. The types swap too: flipping `[1, "a"]` gives `["a", 1]`, typed `[string, number]`.
challenges.firstHint: Destructuring in the parameter list names both items at once: `([first, second]: [A, B])`. The annotation goes after the whole pattern, not inside it.

challenges.title: Free on both calendars
challenges.prompt: Two people list the days of the month they are free, each list sorted from low to high with no repeats. Write `freeBoth(mine: readonly number[], yours: readonly number[]): number[]`, returning the days on both lists, in order. Walk the two lists together with one index each. When the two days match, keep the day and move both indexes; otherwise move only the index that points at the smaller day.
challenges.firstHint: Both lists are sorted, so the smaller of the two current days cannot turn up later in the other list. Step past it and compare again. Stop as soon as either list runs out.

challenges.title: Header row and the rest
challenges.prompt: A CSV file parsed into rows starts with a row of column names. Write `splitHeader(rows: string[][]): { header: string[]; body: string[][] }`, returning the first row as `header` and every later row in `body`. Use one array destructuring with a rest element, and give the header a default of `[]`, so a file with no rows at all gives two empty lists.
challenges.firstHint: In `const [first, ...rest] = list`, `first` takes item 0 and `rest` collects every item after it into a new array. A default after `=` inside the pattern applies when the item is missing.

challenges.title: The longer of two
challenges.prompt: Write `longer<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T`, returning whichever argument has the greater `length`, or `a` when the two tie. The constraint lets the function read `.length` on anything that has one, so the same function works for two strings and for two arrays, and the caller gets back the type they passed in.
challenges.firstHint: `T extends { length: number }` accepts strings, arrays and any object with a numeric `length`. Inside the function you may read `a.length` and `b.length`, and returning `a` or `b` keeps the caller’s own type.

challenges.title: Most urgent first
challenges.prompt: Declare `type Priority = "high" | "medium" | "low"` and an interface `Task` with a `title` string and a `priority`. Write `byPriority(tasks: readonly Task[]): Task[]`, returning a new list with the high tasks first, then medium, then low, each group in its original order. Sorting the words alphabetically would give high, low, medium, so rank them with a `Record<Priority, number>` and compare the ranks.
challenges.firstHint: Give each priority a number, `high: 0`, `medium: 1`, `low: 2`, and subtract the ranks in the comparator. `sort` keeps equal items in their original order, and `[...tasks]` gives you an array you are allowed to sort.

challenges.title: Only the active ones
challenges.prompt: Users, products and sessions all carry an `active` flag. Write `onlyActive<T extends { active: boolean }>(items: T[]): T[]`, keeping the items whose `active` is `true`, in their original order. Each item keeps its other properties: filtering users gives back users, not bare `{ active: boolean }` objects.
challenges.firstHint: Without a type parameter the result would be `{ active: boolean }[]`, and the caller would lose every other property. With `T extends { active: boolean }` you can read `item.active` and still return `T[]`.

challenges.title: Only on weekdays
challenges.prompt: `Day` is a union of seven short day names, `"mon"` to `"sun"`. Declare `type Weekday = Exclude<Day, "sat" | "sun">`, which leaves the five working days. Then write `isWeekday(day: Day): day is Weekday`, returning `true` from Monday to Friday and `false` at the weekend. The return type tells the compiler that a day which passes the check is a `Weekday`.
challenges.firstHint: `Exclude<Day, "sat" | "sun">` removes two members from the union, so you never write the five working days out by hand. At runtime the check is plain: a day is a weekday when it is neither `"sat"` nor `"sun"`.

challenges.title: Path up to the root
challenges.prompt: Each `Folder` has a `name` and a `parent`, which is another folder, or `null` for the root. Write `pathOf(folder: Folder): string`, returning every name from the root down to the folder, joined with `/`. Walk up with a `while` loop that follows `parent` until it reaches `null`. The condition `current !== null` narrows `current` to a `Folder` inside the loop, so reading `current.name` compiles.
challenges.firstHint: Type the loop variable as `Folder | null` so it can hold the root’s `null` parent. Add each name at the front with `unshift`, or collect them and reverse once at the end.

challenges.title: Playlist length
challenges.prompt: Track lengths are written as minutes and seconds, such as `"3:05"`. Write `playlistSeconds(tracks: string[]): number`, adding up the length of every track in seconds with `reduce`. `playlistSeconds(["3:05", "0:55"])` gives 240. Minutes can run past 59, as in `"72:00"`, and an empty playlist lasts 0 seconds.
challenges.firstHint: `"3:05".split(":")` gives `["3", "05"]`, which is still text, and `Number("05")` is 5. Start `reduce` at `0`: without it an empty list throws, and the first track stays a string.

challenges.title: Price the basket
challenges.prompt: A shop keeps its prices in cents in a `Map` from product name to price. Write `basketTotal(prices: ReadonlyMap<string, number>, basket: string[]): number`, adding up the price of every product in the basket with `reduce`. A product named twice is paid for twice. When a product has no price, the basket cannot be priced: throw an `Error` with the message `No price for <product>`, such as `No price for cake`.
challenges.firstHint: `prices.get(product)` is typed `number | undefined`. Check for `undefined` before you add, and after the check the compiler knows the price is a number. Start `reduce` at `0` so an empty basket totals 0.

challenges.title: Select and deselect
challenges.prompt: A photo grid keeps the ids of the selected photos in a `Set`. Write `toggle(selected: ReadonlySet<string>, id: string): Set<string>`, returning a new Set with `id` removed when it was selected and added when it was not. The parameter is a `ReadonlySet`, so `add` and `delete` do not exist on it: copy it into a new `Set` and change the copy.
challenges.firstHint: `new Set(selected)` copies a Set, and the copy has `add` and `delete`. `has` tells you which of the two to call.

challenges.title: Sort by a column
challenges.prompt: A table shows `Player` rows with a `name`, a `score` and a `country`. Write `sortRows(rows: readonly Player[], column: keyof Player): Player[]`, returning a new array sorted from low to high by the chosen column: numbers by value, text in character order. `keyof Player` is the union `"name" | "score" | "country"`, so a column that does not exist will not compile. Rows with equal values keep their order.
challenges.firstHint: `a[column]` is typed `string | number`, and `<` and `>` compare two numbers by value and two strings by character code. Return `-1`, `1` or `0`. Copy with `[...rows]` first: the parameter is readonly, so `rows.sort` does not compile.

challenges.title: Is it a theme colour?
challenges.prompt: A theme offers three accent colours, listed once as `const ACCENTS = ["teal", "coral", "gold"] as const`. `as const` keeps the exact words, and `type Accent = (typeof ACCENTS)[number]` turns them into the union `"teal" | "coral" | "gold"`. Write `isAccent(value: string): value is Accent`, returning `true` for exactly those three words. A user setting that passes the check can then be stored as an `Accent` with no cast.
challenges.firstHint: `ACCENTS.includes(value)` does not compile: the array only accepts its three words, and `value` can be any string. Widen the array for the check, `(ACCENTS as readonly string[]).includes(value)`, or compare the value with each word in turn.

challenges.title: Tick off a todo
challenges.prompt: Write `markDone(todos: readonly Todo[], id: number): Todo[]`, returning a new list in which the todo with that `id` has `done: true` and every other todo is unchanged. Build the changed todo as a new object with spread, so the caller’s todos stay as they were. An id that matches nothing gives back an equal list. `Todo` is declared for you.
challenges.firstHint: In `{ ...todo, done: true }` the spread copies every property first, and `done: true` then overwrites one of them. Writing `todo.done = true` would change the caller’s object as well.

challenges.title: Trim blank lines
challenges.prompt: Write `trimBlank(lines: readonly string[]): string[]`, returning the lines without the blank ones at the start and at the end. A blank line is empty or holds only spaces. Blank lines between two lines of text stay. Keep one index at each end, move each inward in a `while` loop for as long as it points at a blank line, then copy what lies between them with `slice`.
challenges.firstHint: Check the index before you read the line: when every line is blank, `start` walks off the end, and `lines[start]` is then `undefined`. `slice(start, end + 1)` includes the line at `end`.

challenges.title: Where a value starts and ends
challenges.prompt: A sorted list keeps equal values next to each other. Write `spanOf(sorted: readonly number[], value: number): [number, number] | null`, returning the first and the last index of `value` as a tuple, or `null` when the value is not in the list. Put one index at each end and move each inward for as long as it does not point at the value.
challenges.firstHint: Walk `start` forward while it is at or before `end` and `sorted[start]` is not the value. Then walk `end` back while `sorted[end]` is not the value. If `start` ends up past `end`, the value was never there.

challenges.title: Every reading in Celsius
challenges.prompt: Weather stations report in Celsius or in Fahrenheit, and each `Reading` names its scale in `unit`. Write `toCelsius(readings: readonly Reading[]): number[]`, returning one Celsius value per reading with `map`. A Celsius reading stays as it is. A Fahrenheit one becomes `(value - 32) * 5 / 9`, rounded to one decimal place with `Math.round(celsius * 10) / 10`.
challenges.firstHint: Check `reading.unit` inside the callback. `map` needs a number back for every reading, the Celsius ones included, or that slot ends up `undefined`. Round only the converted value.

challenges.title: Alternate two playlists
challenges.prompt: A party playlist takes turns between two guests’ lists: a song from `a`, then one from `b`, then the next from `a`, and so on. When one list runs out, the rest of the other follows in order. Write `alternate<T>(a: readonly T[], b: readonly T[]): T[]`, with one index for each list. The type parameter lets it work for song titles, ids or any other items, as long as both lists hold the same kind.
challenges.firstHint: Inside the loop, take `a[i]` when `i` is still in range, then `b[j]` when `j` is. Each index moves only when its own list gave an item, so the longer list carries on after the shorter one ends. Test the index, not the item: a song called `""` or an id of `0` is still an item.

challenges.title: Change one field
challenges.prompt: A shop admin edits one field of a product at a time. Write `setField<K extends keyof Product>(product: Product, key: K, value: Product[K]): Product`, returning a new product with that one field changed. The types tie the value to the key: `setField(mug, "price", 5)` compiles and `setField(mug, "price", "5")` does not. Build the new product with spread, and leave the original as it is.
challenges.firstHint: A key in square brackets inside an object literal is a computed key: `{ [key]: value }` uses whatever `key` holds as the property name. Spread the product first and put `[key]: value` after it, so the new value wins.

challenges.title: Check the JSON first
challenges.prompt: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, so the compiler believes whatever you say came back. Write `isUser(value: unknown): value is User`, returning `true` only for an object whose `name` is a string and whose `age` is a number. Then write `readUser(text: string): User | null`: parse the text, which is always valid JSON, and return the result when `isUser` accepts it, or `null` when it does not. `null` is valid JSON too, and `typeof null` is `"object"`.
challenges.firstHint: Store the parsed result as `unknown`, not `any`, and the compiler makes you check it before you use it. After `typeof value === "object" && value !== null`, the test `"name" in value` lets you read `value.name` and check its type with `typeof`.

challenges.title: Is the profile complete?
challenges.prompt: A `Profile` needs only a `name`: the `email` and the `phone` are optional. `Required<Profile>` is the same type with every property required. Write `isComplete(profile: Profile): profile is Required<Profile>`, returning `true` when the email and the phone are both filled in, which means present and not an empty string. After `if (isComplete(profile))`, the compiler reads `profile.email` as a `string` instead of `string | undefined`.
challenges.firstHint: A type predicate is still a boolean at runtime, and the checks return `true` or `false`. `profile.email && profile.phone` gives back one of the strings instead, and the compiler refuses a string where the predicate needs a boolean. Compare each field with `undefined` and with `""`.

challenges.title: Data or an error
challenges.prompt: A batch of API replies holds two shapes: `{ data }` when a call worked and `{ error }` when it failed. There is no shared `kind` field to compare, so narrow with the `in` operator: inside `if ("error" in reply)`, TypeScript knows `reply` is the error shape. Write `errorsOf(replies: readonly Reply[]): string[]`, returning every error message, in order.
challenges.firstHint: `reply.error` does not compile on a plain `Reply`, because the data shape has no `error`. The check `"error" in reply` narrows it. Type the `filter` callback as `reply is { error: string }`, and the `map` after it can read `.error`.

challenges.title: Every nth item
challenges.prompt: A video editor builds a preview from every third frame of a clip. Write `everyNth<T>(items: readonly T[], n: number): T[]`, returning the items at positions `n`, `2n`, `3n` and so on, counting from 1. In a `for` loop that means starting at index `n - 1` and adding `n` each time. The type parameter hands the caller back the item type they passed in. An `n` below 1 gives `[]`.
challenges.firstHint: The third item sits at index 2, so the first index is `n - 1`, and `i += n` jumps straight to the next one. Check `n < 1` first: with `n` at 0, `i += n` never moves and the loop never ends.

challenges.title: Move to a new city
challenges.prompt: Write `moveTo(user: User, city: string): User`, returning a new user whose address has the new `city` and keeps its `street`. The user you were given must not change, and neither must its address. Spread copies one level only: `{ ...user }` is a new user that still points at the old `address` object, so the address needs a spread of its own.
challenges.firstHint: Check the original after a run: if `user.address.city` changed, your copy still shares the address object. A second spread, nested inside the first, gives the address a copy of its own.

challenges.title: Keep the newest version
challenges.prompt: A sync job receives records that can repeat: the same `id` may arrive more than once with a different `version`. Write `latest<T extends { id: string; version: number }>(records: readonly T[]): T[]`, keeping one record per id: the one with the highest version. When two share the highest version, keep the one that came first. Return the records in the order their ids first appeared. A `Map` from id to record does both jobs: `set` on a key it already holds replaces the value and leaves the key where it was.
challenges.firstHint: Read what the map already holds with `byId.get(record.id)`. Store the new record only when there is nothing yet or its version is strictly higher, so a tie keeps the first. The constraint lets you read `id` and `version`, and `T` hands the caller back their own record type with every other field.

challenges.title: The next traffic light
challenges.prompt: A traffic light shows `"red"`, then `"green"`, then `"amber"`, then red again. Declare `type Light = "red" | "green" | "amber"` and a table `const NEXT: Record<Light, Light>` that maps each light to the one after it. Then write `nextLight(light: Light, steps: number): Light`, moving through the table `steps` times. Typed as `Record<Light, Light>`, the table cannot leave a light out or misspell one without a compile error.
challenges.firstHint: Look the next light up with `NEXT[current]`. The `Record<Light, Light>` type makes the compiler check that every light has an entry and that every value is a real light. A `for` loop that runs `steps` times does the moving.

challenges.title: Only the clicks
challenges.prompt: An analytics script records `UiEvent` values: clicks with an `x` and a `y`, and key presses with a `key`. Declare `type Click = Extract<UiEvent, { kind: "click" }>`: the members of the union that fit that shape. Then write `clicks(events: readonly UiEvent[]): Click[]`, returning the clicks in their original order. Give `filter` a callback whose return type is the type predicate `event is Click`, so the array it hands back holds only clicks.
challenges.firstHint: `Extract` is the opposite of `Exclude`: it keeps the members of a union that are assignable to the second argument. The runtime check is one comparison on `event.kind`. The predicate return type tells the compiler what that comparison proved.

challenges.title: One line per order
challenges.prompt: An order list shows each order on one line, such as `#12 Ada, 3 items`. Write `orderLine(order: Order): string`. Destructure the `id`, the customer’s `name` and the `items` in the parameter list: a nested pattern reaches into `customer`. Write `item` for exactly one item and `items` for any other count, 0 included.
challenges.firstHint: In `customer: { name }`, the colon opens a nested pattern: `name` comes from `order.customer.name`, and no `customer` variable is created. A template literal builds the line: `` `#${id} ${name}, ${items.length} ${word}` ``.

challenges.title: Pages as ranges
challenges.prompt: A print dialog shows the pages you picked as ranges: `[1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10]` reads `"1-3, 7-8, 10"`. Write `toRanges(pages: readonly number[]): string`. The pages are sorted, with no repeats. Keep two indexes: `start` on the first page of a run, and `end`, which moves forward while the next page is one more than the page at `end`. Write the run as `"start-end"`, or as one number when it holds a single page, then begin the next run after `end`. Join the runs with `", "`. No pages give `""`.
challenges.firstHint: A run goes on while `pages[end + 1] === pages[end] + 1`. When it stops, the run covers `pages[start]` to `pages[end]`, and the next run starts at `end + 1`.

challenges.title: Who reached the pass mark
challenges.prompt: Exam results arrive as a `Record<string, number>` from each student’s name to their score. Write `passed(scores: Record<string, number>, mark: number): string[]`, returning the names of the students who scored `mark` or more, in the order the record lists them. Loop over `Object.entries(scores)` with `for...of`, and destructure each entry in the loop head into a name and a score.
challenges.firstHint: `Object.entries` turns the record into `[name, score]` pairs. Destructuring the pair in the loop head, `for (const [name, score] of …)`, names both parts, so the body reads `score >= mark` instead of `entry[1] >= mark`.

challenges.title: Pin a chat to the top
challenges.prompt: A messaging app lets you pin one chat above the others. Write `pinToTop(chats: readonly string[], chat: string): string[]`, returning a new list with `chat` first and every other chat after it, in the same order as before. Build it as `[chat, ...rest]`, where `rest` is the list without that chat. A chat that is not in the list is not added: return a copy of the list as it is.
challenges.firstHint: `filter` gives you the list without the pinned chat, and a spread puts that list after it in a new array. Check `includes` first, or a chat that was never in the list would appear at the top.

challenges.title: Rank the scores
challenges.prompt: A quiz keeps its scores in an object from each player’s name to their points. Write `ranked(scores: Record<string, number>): [string, number][]`, returning `[name, points]` pairs from the most points to the fewest. `Object.entries(scores)` gives you the pairs; sort them by their second item. Players on the same points keep the order the object lists them in.
challenges.firstHint: Each entry is a `[name, points]` pair, so the points sit at index 1. A compare function that subtracts the first pair’s points from the second’s sorts from high to low, and a difference of 0 keeps the order. `Object.entries` builds a new array, so sorting it leaves `scores` alone.

challenges.title: Headers until the blank line
challenges.prompt: An HTTP response starts with header lines such as `Content-Type: text/html`, then one blank line (`""`), then the body. Write `readHeaders(lines: readonly string[]): Record<string, string>`, reading from the top with a `while` loop until it reaches the blank line or runs out of lines. Split each header at its first `": "`: the name before it, in lower case, is the key, and everything after it is the value. Nothing after the blank line is read, even when it looks like a header.
challenges.firstHint: `indexOf(": ")` finds only the first separator, so a value that holds its own `": "` stays whole. `slice(0, at)` is the name and `slice(at + 2)` the value. `split(": ")` would cut such a value in pieces.

challenges.title: A type from a function
challenges.prompt: A till reads each receipt line with `parseLine`, written for you, which returns `{ name, qty, cents }`. Declare `type Line = ReturnType<typeof parseLine>`, so the type follows the function if it ever changes. Then write `orderTotal(lines: readonly Line[]): number`, returning the sum of `qty * cents` over every line, in cents. Use `reduce` with a start value of `0`.
challenges.firstHint: `typeof parseLine` is the type of the function, and `ReturnType` takes the type of what it returns: `{ name: string; qty: number; cents: number }`. Keep the `0`: without a start value, `reduce` throws on an empty list.

challenges.title: Wait times between retries
challenges.prompt: A client that cannot reach the server waits before it tries again, and doubles the wait each time. Write `retryDelays(first: number, cap: number): readonly number[]`, listing the waits in milliseconds: `first`, then twice that, and so on while the wait is no more than `cap`. `retryDelays(100, 1000)` gives `[100, 200, 400, 800]`. You do not know the count in advance, so use a `while` loop. A `first` of 0 or less never grows, so return `[]` for it. The `readonly` return type stops a caller from pushing a wait of their own.
challenges.firstHint: Build the list in an ordinary `number[]` and return it: a mutable array is assignable to `readonly number[]`, and the caller sees only the read-only type. Check `first <= 0` before the loop, or it never ends.

challenges.title: Each stop and the next
challenges.prompt: A bus route is a list of stops in order. Write `legs(stops: readonly string[]): [string, string][]`, returning one `[from, to]` pair per leg: each stop with the stop after it. `legs(["Depot", "Park", "Station"])` gives `[["Depot", "Park"], ["Park", "Station"]]`. Use a `for` loop whose index stops one short of the last stop. A route with fewer than two stops has no legs.
challenges.firstHint: Annotate the result as `[string, string][]`, a list of pairs. Without that, TypeScript infers `[a, b]` as `string[]`, which may hold any number of strings. Stop the loop at `i < stops.length - 1`, so `stops[i + 1]` always exists.

challenges.title: Save a new todo
challenges.prompt: A todo app hands out ids itself, so a new todo arrives without one. `Todo` has an `id`, a `title` and a `done` flag. Declare `type NewTodo = Omit<Todo, "id">`, then write `addTodo(todos: readonly Todo[], draft: NewTodo): Todo[]`. It returns a new list with the draft added at the end under the next id: one more than the highest id in the list, or `1` when the list is empty. Build the new todo with spread and leave the list you were given as it is.
challenges.firstHint: `Omit<Todo, "id">` is `Todo` without its `id`, so a caller cannot pick one. `Math.max(0, ...todos.map((todo) => todo.id))` is the highest id, or 0 for an empty list. The last todo is not always the one with the highest id.

challenges.title: A setting or its default
challenges.prompt: An app stores only the settings a user has changed, as a `Partial<Settings>`. Write `settingOr<K extends keyof Settings>(saved: Partial<Settings>, key: K): Settings[K]`, returning the saved value for `key`, or the one in `DEFAULTS` when nothing is saved. The return type `Settings[K]` means the type of that one setting, so `settingOr(saved, "sounds")` is a `boolean` and `settingOr(saved, "fontSize")` is a `number`. A saved `false` or `0` is a real choice: keep it.
challenges.firstHint: `K extends keyof Settings` makes `key` one of `"theme"`, `"fontSize"` or `"sounds"`, and `Settings[K]` looks up the type that key holds. At runtime, `??` falls back only on `undefined` and `null`. `||` would also replace a saved `false`, and switch the sounds back on.

challenges.title: Sort titles, ignoring case
challenges.prompt: A reading list shows its titles from A to Z. `sort` with no compare function orders by character code, where every capital letter comes before every lower-case one, so `"Zebra"` lands before `"apple"`. Write `sortTitles(titles: readonly string[]): string[]`, returning a new array sorted by the lower-case form of each title, compared with `<` and `>`. Titles that differ only in case keep their original order.
challenges.firstHint: Lower-case both titles inside the compare function and return `-1`, `1` or `0`. The `0` matters: it tells `sort` to keep the two titles in their order. Copy with `[...titles]` first, because `sort` works in place and the parameter is read-only.

challenges.title: Squares visited
challenges.prompt: A robot on a grid logs each position it passes as an `[x, y]` pair, and it can cross the same square more than once. Write `visited(path: readonly [number, number][]): number`, returning how many different squares it visited. `new Set(path)` does not work here: two arrays holding the same numbers are still two different objects, so the Set keeps both. Turn each pair into a text key such as `"2,3"` and count the keys in a `Set<string>`.
challenges.firstHint: A Set compares objects by identity and strings by value. `` `${x},${y}` `` gives the same text for the same square every time, and the comma keeps `[1, 23]` apart from `[12, 3]`. `seen.size` is the count.

challenges.title: Swap in the edited item
challenges.prompt: An edit form saves one item of a list. Write `replaceById<T extends { id: number }>(items: readonly T[], edited: T): T[]`, returning a new array in which the item with the same `id` as `edited` is replaced by it. Every other item stays as it was, in the same place. When no item has that id, the new array holds the same items as before. Use `map`: the constraint lets you read `.id`, and `T` keeps the caller’s own item type on the way out.
challenges.firstHint: `map` returns one result per item, so the length and the order stay the same without any extra work. Compare `item.id === edited.id` and return either `edited` or `item`. Changing `items[i]` would edit the caller’s array too.

challenges.title: Fall back to a default
challenges.prompt: Write `orDefault<T>(value: T | null | undefined, fallback: T): T`, returning the value unless it is null or undefined, in which case the fallback. Zero, an empty string and false are real values and come back as they are.
challenges.firstHint: The point of the function is that the answer can no longer be missing, which is why the return type is the plain type.

challenges.title: First item
challenges.prompt: Write `first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined`, returning the opening item of an array of anything, and `undefined` when there is nothing in it. One type parameter is enough — the caller should get back the type they put in.
challenges.firstHint: A type parameter is a type the caller fills in, so the answer keeps whatever went in instead of widening to any.

challenges.title: Freeze a copy
challenges.prompt: Declare a mapped type `Frozen<T>` that keeps every property of `T` with its type but marks it `readonly`, then write `freezeCopy<T extends object>(source: T): Frozen<T>` building a fresh object from `Object.entries` in a `for-of` loop and freezing it with `Object.freeze` before returning it. `freezeCopy({ a: 1 })` gives an object equal to `{ a: 1 }` that is not the same object, and assigning to its `a` is a compile error.
challenges.firstHint: A mapped type walks keyof T and can put a modifier in front of every property it produces; the loop does the same job at runtime, one entry at a time.

challenges.title: Greeting with a default
challenges.prompt: Write `greet(name: string, greeting?: string): string`, returning the greeting, a comma, the name and an exclamation mark — `Hello, Ada!`. The greeting is optional and falls back to `Hello`, but an empty greeting that was actually passed is used as given.
challenges.firstHint: A default value in the parameter list is what makes an argument optional — and only a missing one is replaced by it.

challenges.title: Group by key
challenges.prompt: Write `groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(items: T[], keyOf: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]>`, collecting every item under the key the callback gives it, with a `for-of` loop. The constraint keeps the key something an object can be indexed by. `groupBy([1, 2, 3, 4], n => n % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd")` gives `{ odd: [1, 3], even: [2, 4] }`, and an empty list gives an empty object.
challenges.firstHint: PropertyKey is the union of everything that can name a property, and constraining K to it is what makes Record<K, ...> legal.

challenges.title: Hide the password
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Account` with a numeric `id` and string `email` and `password`, then write `publicUser(account: Account): Omit<Account, "password">`, returning a copy with the password removed rather than blanked.
challenges.firstHint: Omit builds a new type from an existing one with named properties taken out, and rest destructuring does the same to the value.

challenges.title: Inferred total
challenges.prompt: Write `totalLength(words: string[]): number`, adding up the length of every word. Start the running total at `0` without a type annotation and let the compiler infer `number` from that starting value, then add each length in a `for-of` loop. `totalLength(["hi", "there"])` gives 7, and an empty list gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: A variable initialised with a number is a number from then on, so the loop can add to it without any annotation.

challenges.title: Lowest and highest
challenges.prompt: Write `minMax(values: number[]): [number, number]`, returning the smallest and the largest value as a tuple, found in a single `for` loop over the list. `minMax([3, 1, 2])` gives `[1, 3]`, a single value is both ends, and an empty list gives `[0, 0]`.
challenges.firstHint: Start both ends at the first value rather than at zero, or a list of negative numbers reports a maximum it never held.

challenges.title: Memoized run
challenges.prompt: Declare `type Output<F> = F extends (arg: number) => infer R ? R : never`, pulling the return type out of a function type with `infer`, then write `runMemoized<F extends (arg: number) => unknown>(fn: F, inputs: number[]): Output<F>[]`. Loop over the inputs with a `Map` as a cache, so an input seen before reuses the stored result instead of calling `fn` again, and return the results in input order. `runMemoized(n => n * 2, [1, 1, 2])` gives `[2, 2, 4]` and calls `fn` twice.
challenges.firstHint: infer names the part of the type you want to capture, and the conditional resolves to it whenever F matches the function shape.

challenges.title: Mixed total
challenges.prompt: Write `mixedTotal(values: (string | number)[]): number`, walking the list with `for-of` and adding each number as it is and each string as its length. Reading `.length` needs the value narrowed to a string first. `mixedTotal([1, "abc", 2])` gives 6, and an empty list gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Inside the loop the value is still the whole union, and a typeof check is what splits it into the two cases.

challenges.title: Only the files
challenges.prompt: Declare interfaces `FileEntry` (`kind: "file"`, a `name` and a numeric `size`) and `FolderEntry` (`kind: "folder"` and a `name`), plus the union `type Entry = FileEntry | FolderEntry`. Write `isFile(entry: Entry): entry is FileEntry`, then use it in `onlyFiles(entries: Entry[]): FileEntry[]` to keep the files in their original order. `onlyFiles([{ kind: "file", name: "a.txt", size: 3 }, { kind: "folder", name: "src" }])` gives just the file.
challenges.firstHint: The predicate's return type is what lets filter hand back FileEntry[] instead of the union you started with.

challenges.title: Only the strings
challenges.prompt: Write `isString(value: unknown): value is string`, then use it in `onlyStrings(values: unknown[]): string[]` to keep only the strings from a mixed list, in their original order. Without the predicate on the first, what the second filters out stays unknown to the compiler.
challenges.firstHint: A predicate returns a plain boolean at runtime; its return type is what tells the compiler what a true answer proves.

challenges.title: Optional nickname
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `User` with a required `name` and an optional `nickname`, both strings, then write `displayName(user: User): string` returning the nickname when the property is there and the name when it is not. A nickname that is present but empty still wins.
challenges.firstHint: Two fallback operators look interchangeable here and are not: one gives way on any falsy value, the other only on null and undefined.

challenges.title: Pad a readonly list
challenges.prompt: Write `padScores(scores: readonly number[], size: number): number[]`, returning a copy of the scores with zeros added at the end until it holds `size` values. The parameter is readonly, so `push` is not available on it and the copy has to be made with spread first. `padScores([7, 9], 4)` gives `[7, 9, 0, 0]`, and a list already at or beyond the size comes back as a plain copy.
challenges.firstHint: The compiler removes every mutating method from a readonly array, so the only array you can push onto is the one you build yourself.

challenges.title: Padded id
challenges.prompt: Write `idText(id: string | number): string`. A number comes back as text padded with leading zeros to four characters; a string comes back untouched. A number already four characters or longer keeps its own length.
challenges.firstHint: A union has to be split before either half can be used, and a typeof check is what tells the compiler which one it is holding.

challenges.title: Pair with a sum
challenges.prompt: Write `pairWithSum(sorted: readonly number[], target: number): [number, number] | null`, finding two values in an ascending list that add up to the target with two pointers: one at each end, moved inward in a `while` loop depending on whether the current sum is too small or too large. Return the pair as a tuple, or `null` when there is none. `pairWithSum([1, 2, 3, 4, 6], 6)` gives `[2, 4]`.
challenges.firstHint: The list is sorted, so a sum that is too small can only be fixed by moving the left pointer up, and one that is too large by moving the right pointer down.

challenges.title: Path length
challenges.prompt: Declare a type alias named `Point` for an object with numeric `x` and `y`, then write `pathLength(points: Point[]): number` adding up the straight-line distance between each point and the next with a `for` loop. `pathLength([{ x: 0, y: 0 }, { x: 3, y: 4 }])` gives 5, and fewer than two points gives 0.
challenges.firstHint: Each step of the loop needs the current point and the one before it, so start the index at 1 rather than 0.

challenges.title: Person interface
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Person` with `first` and `last`, both strings, then write `fullName(person: Person): string` joining them with a single space. When either half is empty the space goes too, so no answer ever starts or ends with one.
challenges.firstHint: An interface is a named shape written once above the function, and then used wherever that shape is expected.

challenges.title: Pluck a property
challenges.prompt: Write `pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][]`, collecting one property from every object in the list. The key has to name a property that exists, and what comes back is an array of whatever that property holds.
challenges.firstHint: keyof turns an object type into the union of its property names, and an indexed access type looks up what sits under one.

challenges.title: Pluck all the keys
challenges.prompt: Write `pluckAll<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], keys: K[]): T[K][][]`, returning one row per item with the values of the requested keys in the order asked, built with `map` inside `map`. The indexed access type `T[K]` is whatever those properties hold. `pluckAll([{ id: 1, name: "a" }], ["id", "name"])` gives `[[1, "a"]]`.
challenges.firstHint: Constraining the key to keyof T is what lets the compiler read T[K] and know the type of every value you pluck.

challenges.title: Rotate a list
challenges.prompt: Write `rotate(items: readonly string[]): string[]`, returning a new array with the first item moved to the end. The parameter is readonly, so the array you were handed comes back unchanged; an empty list and a single item both come back as they are.
challenges.firstHint: A readonly array is missing every method that would change it, which is the compiler telling you to build a new one.

challenges.title: Score by player
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Round` with a `player` string and a `points` number, then write `scoreByPlayer(rounds: Round[]): Record<string, number>` adding up the points of every player with a `for-of` loop. A player seen for the first time has no entry yet, so treat the missing value as 0. `scoreByPlayer([{ player: "ada", points: 3 }, { player: "bo", points: 1 }, { player: "ada", points: 2 }])` gives `{ ada: 5, bo: 1 }`.
challenges.firstHint: Reading a key that is not in a Record<string, number> yet gives undefined at runtime, so fall back to zero before adding.

challenges.title: Shipping speed
challenges.prompt: Declare a type alias named `Speed` allowing only `standard`, `express` or `overnight`, then write `shippingDays(speed: Speed, weekend: boolean): number` giving 5, 2 and 1 day respectively, with one extra day when the order was placed at the weekend.
challenges.firstHint: A type alias can list the exact strings that are allowed, which turns a typo into a compile error rather than a bug.

challenges.title: Sort by name
challenges.prompt: Write `sortByName<T extends { name: string }>(items: T[]): T[]`, returning a new array ordered A to Z by `name`. Anything with a name is allowed in, its other properties survive, and the array handed in is not reordered.
challenges.firstHint: Constrain the type parameter to anything carrying a name, and you can read that property while still handing back the caller’s own type.

challenges.title: Split a name
challenges.prompt: Write `splitName(text: string): [string, string]`, returning a tuple of the first word and everything after it. A single word gives an empty second half, an empty string gives two empty halves, and only the first space ever splits.
challenges.firstHint: A tuple type fixes both how many values come back and what sits at each position.

challenges.title: Tag every id
challenges.prompt:
Declare a template literal type `Tag

` for strings shaped `${P}-${number}`, then write `tagAll

(prefix: P, ids: number[]): Tag

[]` building one tag per id in a `for-of` loop with a template string. `tagAll("user", [1, 2])` gives `["user-1", "user-2"]`, and no ids gives an empty list.
challenges.firstHint: A template string built from a P and a number gets the template literal type when the place it goes to expects one, so type the result array before pushing into it.

challenges.title: Take turns
challenges.prompt: Write `takeTurns(waiting: string[], turns: number): string[]`, serving people from a queue in a round robin: the person at the front is served, then goes to the back, until `turns` people have been served. Copy the list first so the caller's array stays as it was. `takeTurns(["ada", "bo"], 3)` gives `["ada", "bo", "ada"]`, and an empty queue gives an empty list however many turns are asked for.
challenges.firstHint: shift on a string[] hands back string | undefined, and the compiler makes you deal with the undefined before the value goes anywhere.

challenges.title: Tally votes
challenges.prompt: Write `tally(votes: string[]): Record<string, number>`, counting how many times each string appears. The result has one key per distinct vote, and an empty list gives an object with no keys at all.
challenges.firstHint: Record describes an object used as a lookup: what the keys are, and what every value stored under them is.

challenges.title: Top three scores
challenges.prompt: Write `topThree(scores: number[]): number[]`, returning the three highest values, largest first. Fewer than three values gives back all of them in order, and the array you were handed must not be reordered in place.
challenges.firstHint: Sort reorders the array it is given, so copy first — and without a comparator it orders numbers as if they were words.

challenges.title: Total expenses
challenges.prompt: Declare an interface named `Expenses` with `rent`, `food` and `travel`, all numbers, then write `totalExpenses(expenses: Expenses): number` adding the three up with a `for-in` loop. The loop variable is a plain `string`, so index the object with it as `keyof Expenses`. `totalExpenses({ rent: 800, food: 250, travel: 50 })` gives 1100.
challenges.firstHint: A for-in key is a string as far as the compiler knows, and a string is not proof that the property exists, until you assert it is one of the interface's keys.

challenges.title: Transform a list
challenges.prompt: Write `transform<T, R>(items: T[], change: (item: T) => R): R[]`, running the callback over every item and collecting the results. The callback takes one argument, and the type it returns is the element type of the array that comes back.
challenges.firstHint: Two type parameters, not one: what the list holds and what the callback hands back are allowed to differ.

challenges.title: Typed slug
challenges.prompt: Write `toSlug(title: string): string`, turning a title into a URL slug: trimmed, lowercased, with every run of spaces replaced by a single dash. An empty string gives an empty string, and a single word comes back as itself.
challenges.firstHint: The whole job is three string operations in a row, and the type is the same going in and coming out.

challenges.title: Values of a type
challenges.prompt: Declare `type TypeName = "string" | "number" | "boolean"` and a conditional type `OfType<N extends TypeName>` that resolves to `string`, `number` or `boolean` for the matching name. Then write `ofType<N extends TypeName>(values: unknown[], name: N): OfType<N>[]`, keeping the values whose `typeof` equals the name, in their original order, with `filter` and a type predicate. `ofType([1, "a", 2, true], "number")` gives `[1, 2]`.
challenges.firstHint: A conditional type is a chain of extends checks that picks one type per name, and the predicate on the filter callback is where the runtime result gets that type.

challenges.title: Write reduce by hand
challenges.prompt: Write `myReduce<T, U>(items: T[], step: (acc: U, item: T) => U, initial: U): U`, folding a list into one value with a plain `for` loop instead of calling `reduce`. The accumulator starts as `initial` and is replaced by what `step` returns for every item. `myReduce([1, 2, 3], (acc, n) => acc + n, 0)` gives 6, and an empty list gives back `initial` untouched.
challenges.firstHint: The item type and the accumulator type are different type parameters, because a sum of numbers can just as well be built into a string.

challenges.title: Zip two lists
challenges.prompt: Write `zip<A, B>(left: A[], right: B[]): [A, B][]`, pairing the items at the same index into tuples with a `for` loop and stopping at the shorter list. `zip([1, 2], ["a", "b"])` gives `[[1, "a"], [2, "b"]]`, and when either list is empty the result is empty.
challenges.firstHint: Two type parameters keep the two lists independent, and the tuple type in the result fixes which one comes first.
